title: Micah - Introduction
content:
Introduction to Micah

Part 1: General Introduction

Outline of Micah

  1. Yahweh announces judgment on his people and their leaders (1–3)
  2. Yahweh promises future restoration and righteous rule (4–5)
  3. Yahweh calls his people to repentance and offers hope (6–7)

What is the Book of Micah about?

This book contains many of Micah’s prophecies. Micah repeated many similar prophecies as found in Isaiah. Micah warned the kingdoms of Israel and Judah that the Assyrians would soon attack them. Micah condemned those who acted unjustly and immorally. He spoke against those who did not work for a living. He also spoke against the false prophets in Israel and Judah. These false prophets were telling the people that Yahweh would never let a foreign kingdom harm or conquer them.

Micah called the people to please Yahweh by living righteous and holy lives. However, the sinful way they lived and the unjust way they treated their fellow countrymen proved that they no longer wanted to obey and honor Yahweh.

How should the title of this book be translated?

Translators may decide to translate the traditional title “The Book of Micah” or just “Micah” in a way that is clearer to the readers. They may decide to call it “The Sayings of Micah.”

Who wrote Micah?

The prophet Micah wrote this book. Micah lived at the same time as Isaiah and Hosea. This was sometime between 750 and 700 B.C., during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. He began prophesying when he lived in the northern kingdom of Israel. Then he moved to the kingdom of Judah.

Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

Who is the deliverer Micah mentions?

Micah frequently mentioned a king who would deliver the people. It is clear that Micah meant the Messiah, the descendant of David who would rule forever, though he never referred to him as the Messiah.

Were the Israelites required to offer sacrifices or live holy lives to please Yahweh?

Many of the Old Testament writers were concerned with offering sacrifices according to the law of Moses. However, Micah explained to the people that Yahweh was pleased only when they offered these sacrifices in faith. Without faith, the sacrifices had no meaning.

Part 3: Important Translation Issues

What does a translator need to know before translating Micah?

Micah did not often explain how his prophecies were historically situated. This may result in the translator failing to understand implicit information unless they understand Micah’s time. It is therefore suggested that translators understand well the history of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

How do I translate passages where the speaker or addressee is not mentioned explicitly?

Micah did not usually say who was speaking or who was being addressed. Reading the verses before and after the quote will often help the reader to understand who is speaking or being addressed. It is acceptable to make this information explicit so the reader can more easily understand it.

“let” and “may”

The ULT uses the English helping verbs “let” and “may” to show that a speaker is expressing a desire that something happen or that someone do something. It uses the verb “let” for more assertive expressions, and it uses the verb “may” for more deferential expressions. For example, when David says in Psalms 69:34 “Let the heavens and the earth praise him,” he means “I want the heavens and the earth to praise him.” Languages that do not have a volitional form might say “The heavens and earth ought to praise him,” or they might use an imperative, “Praise him, heavens and earth!” When Micah says in 5:9 “May your hand rise over your adversaries,” he is being more deferential, even though his wish is urgent, because he is addressing Yahweh, a superior. Languages that do not have a volitional form might say “Yahweh, I desire that your hand rise over your adversaries,” or they might use an imperative with an indication that it is a polite request, “Yahweh, please defeat your adversaries.” Translate this volitional form in the most natural way in your language to indicate that the speaker is expressing what he wants someone to do or what he wishes someone would do.

How should the text of Micah be formatted?

The ULT uses a poetic language style like the Hebrew text. Many languages can do this but some languages will not be able to do this. The ULT also sets apart the poetic portions of the text by setting the poetic lines farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text. With the exception of the first verse, the entire book is indented because the prophecies were written as a series of poems.

title: Micah - Chapter 1 Introduction
content:
Micah 1 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Micah is written mainly in a poetic form. Most of the prophets wrote to either the Northern Kingdom or the Southern Kingdom. Micah wrote to both of them at times without clear distinction, as he did in this chapter.

  1. Yahweh comes to judge the nations (1–5)
  2. Samaria is destroyed because of its sin (6–7)
  3. Micah mourns the coming judgment on Judah (8–16)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Idolatry as prostitution

Samaria’s idols are called a prostitute’s wages, portraying idolatry as unfaithfulness to Yahweh.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

City names

Several times in this chapter, the names of the cities are used to describe their destruction. This sounds unusual in English because of its construction in Hebrew. It contains several “plays on words.” “Lachish will be lashed” is an example of this type of construction. This kind of poetic element rarely carries into other languages but including the information in a footnote may be helpful.

title: Micah 1:1 (#1)
content:
דְּבַר־יְהוָ֣ה ׀ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֗ה אֶל־מִיכָה֙ הַ⁠מֹּ֣רַשְׁתִּ֔י בִּ⁠ימֵ֥י יוֹתָ֛ם אָחָ֥ז יְחִזְקִיָּ֖ה מַלְכֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֑ה אֲשֶׁר־חָזָ֥ה עַל־שֹׁמְר֖וֹן וִ⁠ירֽוּשָׁלִָֽם

"The word of Yahweh that was to Micah the Morashtite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, {and} Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem"

Micah is speaking of himself in the third person as Micah and he to introduce this book.

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Micah 1:1 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־חָזָ֥ה

"which he saw"

The pronoun he refers to Micah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [which Micah saw]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 1:1 (#3)
content:
דְּבַר־יְהוָ֣ה

"The word of Yahweh"

Micah is using the possessive form to describe a word that comes from Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The word from Yahweh]

See: Possession

title: Micah 1:2 (#1)
content:
הַקְשִׁ֖יבִי אֶ֣רֶץ

"pay attention, earth"

Micah is speaking to the earth, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the judgment that Yahweh is about to bring. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the earth. Alternate translation: [everyone on earth should pay attention]

See: Apostrophe

title: Micah 1:2 (#2)
content:
אֶ֣רֶץ וּ⁠מְלֹאָ֑⁠הּ

"earth, and its fullness"

Here, its fullness represents everything and everyone that fills the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [earth, and everything and everyone in it]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 1:2 (#3)
content:
מֵ⁠הֵיכַ֥ל קָדְשֽׁ⁠וֹ

"from the palace of his holiness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of holiness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from his holy palace]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:3 (#1)
content:
כִּֽי־הִנֵּ֥ה

"For behold"

Micah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention for]

See: Foreground Information

title: Micah 1:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠דָרַ֖ךְ עַל־במותי אָֽרֶץ

"and tread on the high places of the earth"

Micah is speaking of Yahweh acting with power over the earth as if he would tread on the high places of the earth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [act with power over even the highest places of the earth]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 1:4 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נָמַ֤סּוּ הֶֽ⁠הָרִים֙ תַּחְתָּ֔י⁠ו

"And the mountains will melt under him"

Micah is speaking of the effect of Yahweh’s powerful presence as if the solid mountains will melt under him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it will be like the mountains will soften and flow out from beneath him]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 1:4 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠עֲמָקִ֖ים יִתְבַּקָּ֑עוּ כַּ⁠דּוֹנַג֙ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י הָ⁠אֵ֔שׁ כְּ⁠מַ֖יִם מֻגָּרִ֥ים בְּ⁠מוֹרָֽד

"and the valleys will split open, like wax from the face of the fire, like waters poured down a steep place"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the comparisons of the wax and the water with the information about the mountains melting as modeled in the UST.

See: Information Structure

title: Micah 1:4 (#3)
content:
כַּ⁠דּוֹנַג֙ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י הָ⁠אֵ֔שׁ

"like wax from the face of the fire"

The point of this comparison is that just as wax melts when it is near a fire, so it will be as if the mountains will melt away because of the power of Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as wax melts when it is near a fire]

See: Simile

title: Micah 1:4 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י הָ⁠אֵ֔שׁ

"from the face of the fire"

Micah is using from the face of as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [melts because of the heat of the fire]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 1:4 (#5)
content:
כְּ⁠מַ֖יִם מֻגָּרִ֥ים בְּ⁠מוֹרָֽד

"like waters poured down a steep place"

The point of this comparison is that just as waters rush swiftly and unstoppably down a steep place, so the will the mountains quickly melt before the powerful presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as swiftly and unstoppably as waters rushing down a steep place]

See: Simile

title: Micah 1:4 (#6)
content:
כְּ⁠מַ֖יִם מֻגָּרִ֥ים בְּ⁠מוֹרָֽד

"like waters poured down a steep place"

The expression poured is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like waters that pour down from a steep place]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 1:5 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠פֶ֤שַׁע יַֽעֲקֹב֙

"because of the transgression of Jacob"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of transgression, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because of how Jacob has rebelled]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:5 (#2)
content:
יַֽעֲקֹב֙

"Jacob"

Here Micah is using the name Jacob to refer to the people of Israel who were all descendants of the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 1:5 (#3)
content:
בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"the house of Israel"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Israel figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 1:5 (#4)
content:
מִֽי־פֶ֣שַׁע יַעֲקֹ֗ב הֲ⁠לוֹא֙ שֹֽׁמְר֔וֹן

"Who {is} the transgression of Jacob? {Is} it not Samaria"

Micah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Samaria is the cause of Jacob’s transgression!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 1:5 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠מִי֙ בָּמ֣וֹת יְהוּדָ֔ה הֲ⁠ל֖וֹא יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם

"And who {are} the high places of Judah? {Is} it not Jerusalem"

Micah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And Jerusalem lead Judah to worship idols on the high places!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 1:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שַׂמְתִּ֥י

"So I will make"

This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh said, “So I will make”]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Micah 1:6 (#2)
content:
לַ⁠גַּי֙ אֲבָנֶ֔י⁠הָ וִ⁠יסֹדֶ֖י⁠הָ

"her stones into the gorge, and her foundations"

The pronoun her refers to the city of Samaria, which Yahweh speaks of as if it were a woman. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Samaria’s stones into the gorge, and Samaria’s foundations]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 1:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־פְּסִילֶ֣י⁠הָ יֻכַּ֗תּוּ

"And all her carved images will be crushed"

The expression crushed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And enemies will crush all Samaria’s carved images]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 1:7 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־אֶתְנַנֶּ֨י⁠הָ֙ יִשָּׂרְפ֣וּ בָ⁠אֵ֔שׁ

"and all her wages will be burned in the fire"

The expression burned is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and fire will burn up all her wages]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 1:7 (#3)
content:
אָשִׂ֣ים שְׁמָמָ֑ה

"I will make a desolation"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of desolation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will completely destroy]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:7 (#4)
content:
יָשֽׁוּבוּ

"they will return"

The pronoun they refers to the idols and treasures that Samaria gathered. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these treasures will be used again]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 1:8 (#1)
content:
אֶסְפְּדָ֣ה וְ⁠אֵילִ֔ילָה

"I shall lament and wail"

The terms lament and wail mean similar things. Micah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I shall greatly mourn]

See: Doublet

title: Micah 1:8 (#2)
content:
אֵילְכָ֥ה שילל וְ⁠עָר֑וֹם

"I shall go barefoot and naked"

Going about without sandals or clothing was a symbolic action by which Micah showed his deep grief and mourning over the coming disaster. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I shall go barefoot and naked to show my grief]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Micah 1:8 (#3)
content:
אֶעֱשֶׂ֤ה מִסְפֵּד֙ כַּ⁠תַּנִּ֔ים

"I shall make a lamentation like the jackals"

The point of this comparison is that just as the jackals make loud, wailing cries, so Micah’s lamentation will be loud and mournful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I shall make a lamentation as loud and mournful as the cries of the jackals]

See: Simile

title: Micah 1:8 (#4)
content:
מִסְפֵּד֙

"a lamentation"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of lamentation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [mournful wailing]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:8 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֖בֶל כִּ⁠בְנ֥וֹת יַעֲנָֽה

"and mourning like the daughters of an owl"

The point of this comparison is that just as the daughters of an owl make mournful, crying sounds, so Micah’s mourning will sound. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and mourning that sounds like the crying of young owls]

See: Simile

title: Micah 1:8 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֖בֶל כִּ⁠בְנ֥וֹת יַעֲנָֽה

"and mourning like the daughters of an owl"

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I shall make mourning like the daughters of an owl]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 1:8 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֖בֶל

"and mourning"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of mourning, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I shall mourn]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:9 (#1)
content:
אֲנוּשָׁ֖ה מַכּוֹתֶ֑י⁠הָ

"her wounds {are} incurable"

Micah is speaking of the destruction that has struck the city as if it were wounds that cannot be healed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the destruction that struck her cannot be undone]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 1:9 (#2)
content:
מַכּוֹתֶ֑י⁠הָ

"her wounds"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wounds, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the places where she is wounded]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:9 (#3)
content:
כִּי־בָ֨אָה֙ עַד־יְהוּדָ֔ה נָגַ֛ע

"for it has come to Judah. It has reached"

The pronoun it refers to the disaster and judgment that Yahweh is bringing. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for this disaster has also come to Judah. This disaster has reached]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 1:9 (#4)
content:
שַׁ֥עַר עַמִּ֖⁠י

"the gate of my people"

Here, gate represents the city of Jerusalem itself, since the gate was the main entrance to the city and the place where it was defended. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the city of my people]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 1:10 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠גַת֙ אַל־תַּגִּ֔ידוּ

"In Gath, do not declare {it"

The word translated as declare sounds like the name of the city, Gath. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Micah 1:10 (#2)
content:
אַל־תַּגִּ֔ידוּ

"do not declare {it"

The pronoun it refers to the news of the coming disaster. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [do not declare the news of the disaster]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 1:10 (#3)
content:
בָּכ֖וֹ אַל־תִּבְכּ֑וּ

"weeping, do not weep"

Micah is repeating forms of the verb weep in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [certainly you should not weep]

See: Reduplication

title: Micah 1:10 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠בֵ֣ית לְעַפְרָ֔ה עָפָ֖ר התפלשתי

"In Beth Leaphrah, roll yourself in the dust"

The name of the town Beth Leaphrah means “house of dust.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Micah 1:10 (#5)
content:
עָפָ֖ר התפלשתי

"roll yourself in the dust"

Rolling oneself in the dust was a symbolic action by which a person showed deep grief and mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [roll yourself in the dust to show your grief]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Micah 1:11 (#1)
content:
שָׁפִ֖יר עֶרְיָה־בֹ֑שֶׁת לֹ֤א יָֽצְאָה֙ יוֹשֶׁ֣בֶת צַֽאֲנָ֔ן מִסְפַּד֙ בֵּ֣ית הָאֵ֔צֶל יִקַּ֥ח מִ⁠כֶּ֖ם

"Shaphir, {in} nakedness of shame. The dweller of Zaanan has not gone out; the mourning of Beth Ezel will take from you"

The name of the town Shaphir means “pleasant” or “beautiful,” the opposite of nakedness and shame. The name of the town Zaanan sounds like the verb “go out.” The name of the town Beth Ezel may mean “house of taking away.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

title: Micah 1:11 (#2)
content:
עֶרְיָה־בֹ֑שֶׁת

"in} nakedness of shame"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of shame, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [shamefully naked]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:11 (#3)
content:
מִסְפַּד֙ בֵּ֣ית הָאֵ֔צֶל

"the mourning of Beth Ezel"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of mourning, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when the people of Beth Ezel mourn, it]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:11 (#4)
content:
יִקַּ֥ח מִ⁠כֶּ֖ם עֶמְדָּתֽ⁠וֹ

"will take from you its standing place"

The pronoun its refers to the town of Beth Ezel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will take from you the standing place of Beth Ezel]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 1:12 (#1)
content:
חָ֥לָֽה לְ⁠ט֖וֹב יוֹשֶׁ֣בֶת מָר֑וֹת

"the dweller of Maroth writhes for {something} good"

The name of the town Maroth sounds like the word for “bitterness,” an opposite of good. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Micah 1:12 (#2)
content:
יָ֤רַד רָע֙ מֵ⁠אֵ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה

"evil has come down from Yahweh"

Micah is using the adjective evil as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [terrible things have come down from Yahweh]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Micah 1:12 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠שַׁ֖עַר יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם

"to the gate of Jerusalem"

Here, the gate represents the city of Jerusalem itself, since the gate was its main entrance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to Jerusalem itself]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 1:13 (#1)
content:
רְתֹ֧ם הַ⁠מֶּרְכָּבָ֛ה לָ⁠רֶ֖כֶשׁ יוֹשֶׁ֣בֶת לָכִ֑ישׁ

"Harness the chariot to the steeds, dweller of Lachish"

The name of the town Lachish sounds like the word for “steed.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Micah 1:13 (#2)
content:
רֵאשִׁ֨ית חַטָּ֥את הִיא֙

"She {was} the beginning of sin"

Even though Micah has addressed the people of Lachish directly as dweller of Lachish, here he speaks of them in the third person as She and then switches back to addressing them as you. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this consistently in the second person. Alternate translation: [You were the beginning of sin]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Micah 1:13 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠בַת־צִיּ֔וֹן

"to daughter Zion"

Micah is speaking of the city of Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and its people as if they were his daughter. This form of expression conveys affection. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to my beloved people of Zion]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 1:13 (#4)
content:
בָ֥⁠ךְ נִמְצְא֖וּ

"in you were found"

The expression were found is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for people found in you]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 1:13 (#5)
content:
פִּשְׁעֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"the transgressions of Israel"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of transgressions, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sinful things that Israel did]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:14 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠כֵן֙

"Therefore"

The word translated as Therefore indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result,]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Micah 1:14 (#2)
content:
תִּתְּנִ֣י שִׁלּוּחִ֔ים עַ֖ל מוֹרֶ֣שֶׁת גַּ֑ת

"you will give dowry gifts to Moresheth Gath"

The town Moresheth Gath is Micah’s hometown. The part of the name Moresheth sounds like the word for “betrothed.” The idea is that, just as a father gave a gift of money (a dowry) along with his daughter to the man she married, the leaders of Jerusalem will have to give tribute to Assyria as they also give them their towns, such as Moresheth Gath.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 1:14 (#3)
content:
בָּתֵּ֤י אַכְזִיב֙ לְ⁠אַכְזָ֔ב

"The houses of Achzib {will} become a deception"

The name of the town Achzib sounds like the word for “deception.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Micah 1:14 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠אַכְזָ֔ב

"will} become a deception"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of deception, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will turn out to be deceptive]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:15 (#1)
content:
עֹ֗ד הַ⁠יֹּרֵשׁ֙ אָ֣בִי לָ֔⁠ךְ יוֹשֶׁ֖בֶת מָֽרֵשָׁ֑ה

"Also a possessor I will bring to you, dweller of Mareshah"

The name of the town Mareshah sounds like the word for possessor. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Micah 1:15 (#2)
content:
כְּב֥וֹד יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"The glory of Israel"

Here, glory represents the honored, important leaders of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [honored ones of Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 1:15 (#3)
content:
עַד־עֲדֻּלָּ֥ם יָב֖וֹא כְּב֥וֹד יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"The glory of Israel will come to Adullam"

By The glory of Israel will come to Adullam, Micah means that the honored leaders of Israel will go into hiding there, just as David once hid in the caves near Adullam to escape his enemies (described in 1 Samuel 22:1). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel’s honored leaders will flee to hide in the caves near Adullam, as David once did]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 1:15 (#4)
content:
כְּב֥וֹד יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"The glory of Israel"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of glory, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The glorious ones of Israel]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:16 (#1)
content:
קָרְחִ֣י וָ⁠גֹ֔זִּי

"Make yourself bald and shave"

The terms translated as Make yourself bald and shave mean similar things. Micah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Shave your head completely bald]

See: Doublet

title: Micah 1:16 (#2)
content:
קָרְחִ֣י וָ⁠גֹ֔זִּי

"Make yourself bald and shave"

Shaving the head completely bald was a symbolic action by which the people would show their deep grief and mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Make yourself bald and shave to show your grief]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Micah 1:16 (#3)
content:
בְּנֵ֖י

"the sons of"

Here the masculine term sons has a generic sense that includes all children whether male or female. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women as modeled in the UST.

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Micah 1:16 (#4)
content:
בְּנֵ֖י תַּעֲנוּגָ֑יִ⁠ךְ

"the sons of your delight"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of delight, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sons who delight you]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:16 (#5)
content:
הַרְחִ֤בִי קָרְחָתֵ⁠ךְ֙ כַּ⁠נֶּ֔שֶׁר

"Enlarge your baldness like the eagle"

The point of this comparison is that just as the eagle has a bare, featherless head, so the people are to make their baldness in mourning complete. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Make your baldness complete, so that your head is as bare as an eagle’s head]

See: Simile

title: Micah 1:16 (#6)
content:
קָרְחָתֵ⁠ךְ֙

"your baldness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of baldness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the bald area on your head]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 1:16 (#7)
content:
כַּ⁠נֶּ֔שֶׁר

"like the eagle"

This word could mean: (1) an eagle, or (2) a vulture. Alternate translation: [like the vulture]

title: Micah 1:16 (#8)
content:
כִּ֥י גָל֖וּ מִמֵּֽ⁠ךְ

"for they have gone into exile from you"

The pronoun they refers to the children whom Micah told the people to mourn for. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for your children have gone into exile from you]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah - Chapter 2 Introduction
content:
Micah 2 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues using poetic forms in communicating that people who take advantage of others are guilty of sin and injustice.

  1. Yahweh condemns those who oppress others (1–5)
  2. Yahweh rebukes those who reject his word (6–11)
  3. Yahweh promises to gather and restore his people (12–13)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Land as inheritance

A family’s fields were an inheritance from Yahweh meant to stay in the family, so seizing them (verses 2, 4) violated covenant order and invited his judgment.

title: Micah 2:1 (#1)
content:
ה֧וֹי חֹֽשְׁבֵי

"Woe to the devisers of"

Micah is using the word Woe to express a strong feeling of warning about the coming judgment on the people he is describing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Great disaster will come upon the devisers of]

See: Exclamations

title: Micah 2:1 (#2)
content:
אָ֛וֶן

"iniquity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of iniquity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is sinful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 2:1 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠פֹ֥עֲלֵי רָ֖ע

"and the workers of evil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of evil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and those who plan to do evil deeds]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 2:1 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠א֤וֹר הַ⁠בֹּ֨קֶר֙ יַעֲשׂ֔וּ⁠הָ כִּ֥י יֶשׁ־לְ⁠אֵ֖ל יָדָֽ⁠ם

"In the light of the morning they do it, for it is in the power of their hand"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because it is in the power of their hand, in the light of the morning they do it]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Micah 2:1 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠אֵ֖ל יָדָֽ⁠ם

"in the power of their hand"

Here, their hand represents their ability to do what they want. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [within their power to do so]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 2:2 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠חָמְד֤וּ שָׂדוֹת֙ וְ⁠גָזָ֔לוּ וּ⁠בָתִּ֖ים וְ⁠נָשָׂ֑אוּ

"And they covet & and seize {them"

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Woe to those who covet fields and seize them and covet houses and take them away]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 2:2 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עָֽשְׁקוּ֙ גֶּ֣בֶר וּ⁠בֵית֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠אִ֖ישׁ וְ⁠נַחֲלָתֽ⁠וֹ

"and his house, and a man and his inheritance"

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And they oppress a man and take away his house, and they oppress a man and take away his inheritance]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 2:2 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נַחֲלָתֽ⁠וֹ

"and his inheritance"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of inheritance, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his inherited property]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 2:3 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠כֵ֗ן

"Therefore"

The term translated as Therefore indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. This marks the shift from the previous accusations to the sentence or judgement about to be pronounced. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Because you do these things]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Micah 2:3 (#2)
content:
הִנְ⁠נִ֥י חֹשֵׁ֛ב

"Behold me, devising"

Yahweh is using Behold me as a common expression to mean that he is about to act. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to devise]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 2:3 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠מִּשְׁפָּחָ֥ה הַ⁠זֹּ֖את

"this clan"

Yahweh is using one part of the nation, this clan to represent all the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of you]

See: Synecdoche

title: Micah 2:3 (#4)
content:
אֲ֠שֶׁר לֹֽא־תָמִ֨ישׁוּ מִ⁠שָּׁ֜ם צַוְּארֹֽתֵי⁠כֶ֗ם

"which you will not remove your necks from there"

Yahweh is speaking of the coming disaster as if it were a heavy yoke on the people, from which you will not remove your necks. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from which you will not be able to free yourselves]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:3 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֤א תֵֽלְכוּ֙ רוֹמָ֔ה

"and you will not walk haughtily"

Yahweh is speaking of behaving or conducting oneself as if it were walking down a path. To walk haughtily means to behave arrogantly or proudly. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will not conduct yourselves proudly]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:4 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֨וֹם הַ⁠ה֜וּא

"In that day"

Micah is using the phrase translated as In that day to introduce a new event. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Micah 2:4 (#2)
content:
יִשָּׂ֧א עֲלֵי⁠כֶ֣ם מָשָׁ֗ל

"someone} will lift up against you a proverb"

Here the word someone refers to the enemies of the people in general, not to any specific person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your enemy will lift up against you a proverb]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 2:4 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נָהָ֨ה נְהִ֤י נִֽהְיָה֙

"and lament a lamentation of a lamentation"

Micah is repeating forms of the word lament in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [and mock you with a mournful dirge]

See: Reduplication

title: Micah 2:4 (#4)
content:
שָׁד֣וֹד נְשַׁדֻּ֔נוּ

"Destroying, we are destroyed"

The people are repeating forms of the same verb, Destroying and we are destroyed, in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [We are utterly destroyed]

See: Reduplication

title: Micah 2:4 (#5)
content:
נְשַׁדֻּ֔נוּ

"we are destroyed"

The expression we are destroyed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has destroyed us]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 2:4 (#6)
content:
חֵ֥לֶק עַמִּ֖⁠י

"The portion of my people"

Micah assumes that readers will know that the phrase portion of my people means the fields and property that Yahweh gave to his people as their inheritance. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The land that my people inherited]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 2:4 (#7)
content:
אֵ֚יךְ יָמִ֣ישׁ

"How he removes {it"

The people are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of dismay and grief at their loss. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Alas, he removes my portion]

See: Exclamations

title: Micah 2:5 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠כֵן֙

"Therefore"

The term translated as Therefore indicates that what follows is a future result of the redistribution of their land. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [As a result,]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Micah 2:5 (#2)
content:
מַשְׁלִ֥יךְ חֶ֖בֶל בְּ⁠גוֹרָ֑ל

"one casting a measuring line by lot"

Micah assumes that readers will know that casting a measuring line by lot refers to the way the tribes received the land in Numbers 26:55. Since Yahweh had promised Abraham the land as an eternal inheritance, Micah knew they would some day return from exile and the land would once again be divided up, but those who Yahweh is judging here will not be a part of that. You could say that explicitly as in the UST if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 2:5 (#3)
content:
בִּ⁠קְהַ֖ל יְהוָֽה

"in the assembly of Yahweh"

Micah is using the possessive form to mean the assembly that belongs to Yahweh, that is, when his people gather once again to divide up the land after returning from exile. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [among Yahweh’s people]

See: Possession

title: Micah 2:6 (#1)
content:
אַל־תַּטִּ֖פוּ יַטִּיפ֑וּ⁠ן

"Do not drip,” they drip"

The pronoun they refers to the false prophets who oppose Micah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [“Do not drip,” the false prophets drip]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 2:6 (#2)
content:
אַל־תַּטִּ֖פוּ יַטִּיפ֑וּ⁠ן לֹֽא־יַטִּ֣פוּ

"Do not drip,” they drip. They do not drip"

Micah is speaking of prophesying as if it words that drip from the prophet’s mouth, letting words fall like rain. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [“Do not pour out words of prophecy,” the false prophets prophesy. They do not prophesy]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:6 (#3)
content:
לֹ֥א יִסַּ֖ג כְּלִמּֽוֹת

"disgraces will not depart"

Here Micah is speaking of disgraces as if they were living things that could depart, or leave on their own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will always be disgraced]

See: Personification

title: Micah 2:7 (#1)
content:
הֶ⁠אָמ֣וּר בֵּֽית־יַעֲקֹ֗ב

"Should it be said, house of Jacob"

Micah is using the question form to rebuke the people for the complacent things they say. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It should not be said, house of Jacob]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 2:7 (#2)
content:
הֶ⁠אָמ֣וּר

"Should it be said"

The expression Should it be said is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Should anyone say]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 2:7 (#3)
content:
בֵּֽית־יַעֲקֹ֗ב

"house of Jacob"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Jacob figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [you Israelites]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:7 (#4)
content:
הֲ⁠קָצַר֙ ר֣וּחַ יְהוָ֔ה

"Is the Spirit of Yahweh short"

Here Micah is speaking of Yahweh being impatient as if his Spirit could be short. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Is Yahweh impatient]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:7 (#5)
content:
הֲ⁠קָצַר֙ ר֣וּחַ יְהוָ֔ה

"Is the Spirit of Yahweh short"

Micah is using the question form to affirm that the Spirit of Yahweh is not impatient. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The Spirit of Yahweh is not impatient!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 2:7 (#6)
content:
אֵ֖לֶּה מַעֲלָלָ֑י⁠ו

"Are these his deeds"

Micah is using the question form to affirm that such calamities are not the kind of thing Yahweh normally does. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [These are not his deeds!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 2:7 (#7)
content:
אֵ֖לֶּה מַעֲלָלָ֑י⁠ו

"Are these his deeds"

The pronoun his refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Are these Yahweh’s deeds]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 2:7 (#8)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֤וֹא דְבָרַ֨⁠י יֵיטִ֔יבוּ עִ֖ם הַ⁠יָּשָׁ֥ר הוֹלֵֽךְ

"Do not my words do good with the one walking uprightly"

Micah is using the question form to affirm that his words which are reflecting Yahweh’s words do good to those who live uprightly. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Surely my words do good with the one walking uprightly.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 2:7 (#9)
content:
הַ⁠יָּשָׁ֥ר הוֹלֵֽךְ

"the one walking uprightly"

Micah is speaking of living or conducting one’s life as if it were walking. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who lives righteously]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:8 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֶתְמ֗וּל עַמִּ⁠י֙

"But recently my people"

This is likely the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh as modeled in the UST.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Micah 2:8 (#2)
content:
עַמִּ⁠י֙ לְ⁠אוֹיֵ֣ב יְקוֹמֵ֔ם

"my people rise up as an enemy"

The pronoun my refers to Yahweh, who begins speaking here about his own people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s people rise up as an enemy]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 2:8 (#3)
content:
עַמִּ⁠י֙ לְ⁠אוֹיֵ֣ב יְקוֹמֵ֔ם

"my people rise up as an enemy"

The point of this comparison is that just as an enemy rises up to attack, so the leaders of Israel who Yahweh calls my people, have turned against Yahweh and have attacked their own defenseless people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [my people attack the way an enemy would attack]

See: Simile

title: Micah 2:8 (#4)
content:
תַּפְשִׁט֑וּ⁠ן

"You strip"

The pronoun You here and in the next verse, refers to the leaders of the Israelite people whom Yahweh has just described as rising up as an enemy against their own people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You leaders of my people strip]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 2:8 (#5)
content:
אֶ֖דֶר

"the splendor"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of splendor, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the most splendid part]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 2:9 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠בֵּ֖ית תַּֽעֲנֻגֶ֑י⁠הָ מֵ⁠עַל֙ עֹֽלָלֶ֔י⁠הָ

"from the house of her delights; from upon her infants"

The pronoun her refers to each of the women among Yahweh’s people whom the leaders are oppressing. He is not speaking about one particular woman but all of the women. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from the houses of their delights; from upon their infants]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 2:9 (#2)
content:
תַּֽעֲנֻגֶ֑י⁠הָ

"her delights"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of delights, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that she delights in]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 2:9 (#3)
content:
הֲדָרִ֖⁠י

"my splendor"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of splendor, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the splendid things I gave them]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 2:10 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠מְּנוּחָ֑ה

"the resting place"

Here Micah is speaking of the land where the people can safely live as if it were a resting place. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the place where you can safely live]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:10 (#2)
content:
טָמְאָ֛ה

"uncleanness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of uncleanness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being unclean]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 2:10 (#3)
content:
תְּחַבֵּ֖ל

"it will destroy"

The phrase it will destroy is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading that scholars have proposed was original, pronouncing the consonants with different vowels. Alternate translation: [it will be destroyed]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Micah 2:10 (#4)
content:
תְּחַבֵּ֖ל

"it will destroy"

The pronoun it refers to the uncleanness of the land, which brings about its destruction. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the land will be destroyed]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 2:10 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠חֶ֥בֶל נִמְרָֽץ

"and a grievous destruction"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of destruction, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will destroy it very severely]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 2:11 (#1)
content:
לוּ־אִ֞ישׁ הֹלֵ֥ךְ ר֨וּחַ֙ וָ⁠שֶׁ֣קֶר כִּזֵּ֔ב

"If a man walking {in} wind and falsehood lied"

Micah is presenting a possible condition, that a person might come speaking lies and promising indulgence. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Suppose a man walking in wind and falsehood lied]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Micah 2:11 (#2)
content:
אִ֞ישׁ הֹלֵ֥ךְ

"a man walking"

Micah is speaking of a person conducting his life as if it were walking down a path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a man who lives]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:11 (#3)
content:
אִ֞ישׁ

"a man"

Micah is not referring to a specific man. He means anyone in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Micah 2:11 (#4)
content:
ר֨וּחַ֙ וָ⁠שֶׁ֣קֶר

"in} wind and falsehood"

Micah is speaking of empty, deceptive speech as wind with no substance. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by empty, deceptive talk]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:11 (#5)
content:
ר֨וּחַ֙ וָ⁠שֶׁ֣קֶר

"in} wind and falsehood"

The phrase wind and falsehood expresses a single idea. The word wind tells more about falsehood, describing it as empty and worthless. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [in worthless lies]

See: Hendiadys

title: Micah 2:11 (#6)
content:
וָ⁠שֶׁ֣קֶר

"and falsehood"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of falsehood, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and speaking false things]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 2:11 (#7)
content:
אַטִּ֣ף לְ⁠ךָ֔ לַ⁠יַּ֖יִן וְ⁠לַ⁠שֵּׁכָ֑ר

"I will drip to you of wine and of beer"

Here the false prophet is speaking of someone who prophesies or preaches as if his words would drip out of his mouth as if they would fall like rain, as in verse 6. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will prophesy to you about wine and beer]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:11 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֥ה מַטִּ֖יף הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּֽה

"he would be the dripper of this people"

Micah is speaking of the false prophet speaking these prophesies that the people want to hear as if he were the dripper whose words would fall like rain. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he would be exactly the sort of prophet this people would welcome]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:12 (#1)
content:
אָסֹ֨ף אֶאֱסֹ֜ף

"Gathering, I will gather"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb gather, in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I will certainly gather]

See: Reduplication

title: Micah 2:12 (#2)
content:
יַעֲקֹ֣ב

"Jacob"

Yahweh is using Jacob, the patriarch, who was also known as Israel, to represent all of his descendants. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

See: Synecdoche

title: Micah 2:12 (#3)
content:
קַבֵּ֤ץ אֲקַבֵּץ֙

"Assembling, I will assemble"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb assemble, in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I will surely assemble]

See: Reduplication

title: Micah 2:12 (#4)
content:
שְׁאֵרִ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"the remnant of Israel"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the remnant that consists of the people of Israel who survive. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the remaining people of Israel]

See: Possession

title: Micah 2:12 (#5)
content:
אֲשִׂימֶ֖⁠נּוּ

"I will set them"

Even though Yahweh is addressing the people directly earlier in this verse, here he speaks about them in the third person as them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could continue to use the second person here. Alternate translation: [I will set you all]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Micah 2:12 (#6)
content:
כְּ⁠צֹ֣אן בָּצְרָ֑ה כְּ⁠עֵ֨דֶר֙ בְּ⁠ת֣וֹךְ הַ⁠דָּֽבְר֔⁠וֹ

"like sheep of Bozrah, like a flock in the midst of its pasture"

The point of this comparison is that just as sheep are gathered together safely into a flock within their pasture, so Yahweh will gather his people together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like sheep of Bozrah gathered safely together, like a flock kept secure within its pasture]

See: Simile

title: Micah 2:13 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠פֹּרֵץ֙

"The breaker"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the leader who goes ahead of the people as if he were The breaker, one who breaks open a way through a barrier. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one who breaks through]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 2:13 (#2)
content:
עָלָ֤ה & לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠הֶ֔ם

"has gone up to the face of them"

Here, to the face of them represents being in front of them or ahead of them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [has gone up in front of them]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 2:13 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יַּעֲבֹ֤ר מַלְכָּ⁠ם֙ לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠הֶ֔ם

"And their king has passed on to the face of them"

Here again, to the face of them represents being in front of them, leading them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And their king has gone ahead of them]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 2:13 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יהוָ֖ה בְּ⁠רֹאשָֽׁ⁠ם

"and Yahweh {is} at their head"

Here, their head represents the leading or foremost position. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh leads the way]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah - Chapter 3 Introduction
content:
Micah 3 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Yahweh judges corrupt leaders and false prophets.

  1. Yahweh condemns the injustice of Israel’s leaders (1–4)
  2. Yahweh exposes the deception of false prophets (5–8)
  3. Yahweh announces judgment on Jerusalem’s rulers (9–12)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Justice

An unjust society was considered to be against the law of Moses. If these kingdoms did not have justice, they were not obedient to Yahweh.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Metaphors

There are vivid pictures used in this chapter which show how the leaders of the people were treating the Israelites. These situations are absurd unless taken as a metaphor.

title: Micah 3:1 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֹמַ֗ר

"And I said"

Micah is using the words And I said to introduce a direct quotation of what he said to the leaders. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Micah 3:1 (#2)
content:
רָאשֵׁ֣י יַעֲקֹ֔ב

"heads of Jacob"

Here, heads represents the leaders of the people and the name Jacob the people of Israel who were all descendants of the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel.. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [leaders of the people of Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 3:1 (#3)
content:
בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"the house of Israel"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Israel figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 3:1 (#4)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא לָ⁠כֶ֔ם לָ⁠דַ֖עַת אֶת־הַ⁠מִּשְׁפָּֽט

"Is it not for you to know justice"

Micah is using the question form to rebuke the leaders and to assert that they are obligated to know justice. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is certainly your responsibility to know justice!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 3:1 (#5)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠מִּשְׁפָּֽט

"justice"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of justice, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how to act justly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 3:2 (#1)
content:
ט֖וֹב וְ⁠אֹ֣הֲבֵי רעה

"good and lovers of evil"

Micah is using the adjectives good and evil as nouns to mean certain kinds of actions. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [doing good things and love doing evil things]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Micah 3:2 (#2)
content:
גֹּזְלֵ֤י עוֹרָ⁠ם֙ מֵֽ⁠עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם וּ⁠שְׁאֵרָ֖⁠ם מֵ⁠עַ֥ל עַצְמוֹתָֽ⁠ם

"tearing their skin from upon them and their flesh from upon their bones"

Here Micah is speaking of the way the leaders oppress the people as if the leaders were butchers tearing their skin from upon them and their flesh from upon their bones. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [brutally oppressing the people, taking everything they have]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 3:2 (#3)
content:
עוֹרָ⁠ם֙ מֵֽ⁠עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם וּ⁠שְׁאֵרָ֖⁠ם מֵ⁠עַ֥ל עַצְמוֹתָֽ⁠ם

"their skin from upon them and their flesh from upon their bones"

The pronouns their and them refer to the victims of the leaders’ oppression. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people’s skin from upon them and the people’s flesh from upon their bones]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 3:2 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠שְׁאֵרָ֖⁠ם מֵ⁠עַ֥ל עַצְמוֹתָֽ⁠ם

"and their flesh from upon their bones"

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and tearing their flesh from upon their bones]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 3:3 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָכְלוּ֮ שְׁאֵ֣ר עַמִּ⁠י֒

"and who have eaten the flesh of my people"

Here Micah is speaking of the way the leaders exploit the people as if the leaders had eaten the flesh of my people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and who have exploited my people]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 3:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עוֹרָ⁠ם֙ מֵ⁠עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֣ם הִפְשִׁ֔יטוּ וְ⁠אֶת־עַצְמֹֽתֵי⁠הֶ֖ם פִּצֵּ֑חוּ

"and their skin from upon them they have stripped, and their bones they have broken"

Here Micah is speaking of how the leaders oppress the people as if the leaders had stripped their skin from upon them and had broken their bones. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they have cruelly oppressed and crushed them]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 3:3 (#3)
content:
הִפְשִׁ֔יטוּ וְ⁠אֶת־עַצְמֹֽתֵי⁠הֶ֖ם פִּצֵּ֑חוּ וּ⁠פָרְשׂוּ֙

"they have stripped, and their bones they have broken, and they have chopped {them} up"

Even though Micah is addressing the leaders of Israel directly (see 3:1), here he is speaking of them in the third person as they. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person for consistency. Alternate translation: [you have stripped, and their bones you have broken, and you have chopped them up]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Micah 3:3 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠פָרְשׂוּ֙ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּ⁠סִּ֔יר וּ⁠כְ⁠בָשָׂ֖ר בְּ⁠ת֥וֹךְ קַלָּֽחַת

"and they have chopped {them} up as {what} is in the pot, and as flesh inside a cauldron"

The point of this comparison is that the leaders treat the people as cruelly as a cook treats the meat that he chops up to cook as what is in the pot and as flesh inside a cauldron. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they have chopped them up as cruelly as a cook chops up the meat that goes in the pot and the flesh inside a cauldron]

See: Simile

title: Micah 3:3 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠כְ⁠בָשָׂ֖ר בְּ⁠ת֥וֹךְ קַלָּֽחַת

"and as flesh inside a cauldron"

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and as they chopped up the flesh to cook inside a cauldron]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 3:4 (#1)
content:
אָ֚ז

"Then"

The word Then indicates that these events will take place at a later time, after the wrongdoing described in the previous verses. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [At a later time]

See: Connect — Sequential Time Relationship

title: Micah 3:4 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יַסְתֵּ֨ר פָּנָ֤י⁠ו מֵ⁠הֶם֙ בָּ⁠עֵ֣ת הַ⁠הִ֔יא כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֵרֵ֖עוּ מַעַלְלֵי⁠הֶֽם

"And he will hide his face from them at that time, just as they have made their deeds evil"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since they have made their deeds evil, he will hide his face from them at that time.]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Micah 3:4 (#3)
content:
יִזְעֲק֣וּ

"they will cry out"

The pronoun they refers to the leaders whom Micah has just finished addressing. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the leaders will cry out]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 3:4 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יַסְתֵּ֨ר פָּנָ֤י⁠ו מֵ⁠הֶם֙

"And he will hide his face from them"

The pronouns he and his refer to Yahweh, and the pronoun them refers to the leaders. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will hide his face from those leaders]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 3:4 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠יַסְתֵּ֨ר פָּנָ֤י⁠ו מֵ⁠הֶם֙

"And he will hide his face from them"

Here, his face represents Yahweh’s favorable attention, so that to hide his face means to refuse to help. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And he will refuse to help them]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 3:5 (#1)
content:
כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה

"Thus says Yahweh"

Micah is using the words Thus says Yahweh to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Micah 3:5 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠מַּתְעִ֣ים אֶת־עַמִּ֑⁠י

"causing my people to wander astray"

Yahweh is speaking of the prophets leading the people into wrong belief and behavior as if the prophets were causing the people to wander astray from the right path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [causing my people to believe and act wrongly]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 3:5 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠נֹּשְׁכִ֤ים בְּ⁠שִׁנֵּי⁠הֶם֙ וְ⁠קָרְא֣וּ שָׁל֔וֹם

"biting with their teeth, then they call out, ‘Peace"

Yahweh is speaking of the practice the prophets had of giving a favorable prophecy to someone in exchange for food or payment as if they were biting with their teeth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when they have been given food to eat, then they call out, ‘Peace!’]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 3:5 (#4)
content:
שָׁל֔וֹם

"Peace"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of Peace, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You will live peacefully and be safe]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 3:5 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠קִדְּשׁ֥וּ עָלָ֖י⁠ו מִלְחָמָֽה

"they consecrate war against him"

The implication is that the prophets perform religious ceremonies to declare a holy war against anyone who does not feed them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they perform ceremonies to declare a holy war against him]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 3:5 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠קִדְּשׁ֥וּ עָלָ֖י⁠ו מִלְחָמָֽה

"they consecrate war against him"

The pronoun they refers to the prophets, and the pronoun him refers to anyone who does not give the prophets food. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the prophets consecrate war against that person]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 3:6 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠כֵ֞ן

"Therefore"

The word Therefore indicates that what follows is the sentence for the crime the prophets are being accused of in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result. Alternate translation: [Because you have done these things]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Micah 3:6 (#2)
content:
לַ֤יְלָה לָ⁠כֶם֙ מֵֽ⁠חָז֔וֹן

"it will be} night for you without vision"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the prophets losing their ability to receive revelation as if they would become blind, saying it would become night for you, a time without vision. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you prophets will receive no more visions]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 3:6 (#3)
content:
מֵֽ⁠חָז֔וֹן

"without vision"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of vision, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [without the ability to see visions]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 3:6 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠חָשְׁכָ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֖ם מִ⁠קְּסֹ֑ם

"and it will be dark for you without divining"

Yahweh assumes that readers will know divining refers to the pagan practice these prophets used to predict the future. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and you will lose the ability you claim you have to predict the future]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 3:6 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בָ֤אָה הַ⁠שֶּׁ֨מֶשׁ֙ עַל־הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֔ים וְ⁠קָדַ֥ר עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֖ם הַ⁠יּֽוֹם

"And the sun will go down on the prophets, and the day will become dark over them"

Yahweh is speaking of the prophets losing his favor and guidance and the gift of true prophesy as if the sun will go down on the prophets, and the day will become dark over them, leaving them in darkness. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the prophets will lose my guidance and the ability to see my revelation]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 3:6 (#6)
content:
עַל־הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֔ים וְ⁠קָדַ֥ר עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֖ם הַ⁠יּֽוֹם

"on the prophets, and the day will become dark over them"

title: Micah - Chapter 4 Introduction
content:
Micah 4 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Yahweh promises the future glory and restoration of his people.

  1. Yahweh establishes his kingdom among the nations (1–5)
  2. Yahweh gathers and restores his people (6–8)
  3. Yahweh delivers Zion through present suffering (9–13)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The remnant

Micah speaks about a future hope and a remnant who will return to their homeland. Verses 1–8 are a vision of the future when God will restore Israel to its former glory. These verses will give hope to those about to be removed from their homeland.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Similar passage

Notice that Micah 4:1–3 is very similar to Isaiah 2:2–4. You may want to translate many of these phrases in a similar way.

Daughter Zion

Yahweh is addressing the people of Jerusalem as “daughter Zion” whom he is personifying as a woman—crying out, in labor, then threshing her enemies.

title: Micah 4:1 (#1)
content:
יִ֠הְיֶה הַ֣ר בֵּית־יְהוָ֤ה נָכוֹן֙ בְּ⁠רֹ֣אשׁ הֶ⁠הָרִ֔ים וְ⁠נִשָּׂ֥א ה֖וּא מִ⁠גְּבָע֑וֹת

Alternate translation: [Yahweh will make the mountain where his temple stands become more important than all the other hills and mountains]

Micah is using the mouth of Yahweh to represent Yahweh himself in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies himself has spoken]

See: Synecdoche

title: Micah 4:5 (#1)
content:
כִּ֚י כָּל־הָ֣⁠עַמִּ֔ים יֵלְכ֕וּ אִ֖ישׁ בְּ⁠שֵׁ֣ם אֱלֹהָ֑י⁠ו

"For all the peoples walk, each one, in the name of his god"

Here, the word walk is used to describe a habitual lifestyle. In this context, to walk … in the name of his god describes the people worshiping and obeying their own false gods. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For all the peoples follow after their own gods] or [For all the peoples serve their own gods]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 4:5 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠שֵׁ֣ם אֱלֹהָ֑י⁠ו

"in the name of his god"

Here, name represents the authority and character of a god. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [under the authority of his god]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 4:5 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנַ֗חְנוּ נֵלֵ֛ךְ

"But we, we will walk"

Micah is stating the pronoun we separately, even though the verb translated as we will walk already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between what the other nations do and what he and his people will do. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [However, my people and I will walk]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 4:5 (#4)
content:
נֵלֵ֛ךְ בְּ⁠שֵׁם־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ

"we will walk in the name of Yahweh our God"

Again, the word walk is used to describe a habitual lifestyle. In contrast to the first phrase in this verse, to we will walk in the name of Yahweh describes the Israelites worshiping and obeying the true God, Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we will live in the manner that Yahweh our God wants]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 4:5 (#5)
content:
יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ

"Yahweh our God"

Micah is not using this possessive form our God to indicate that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather, they are using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship, including himself. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom we worship]

See: Possession

title: Micah 4:6 (#1)
content:
אֹֽסְפָה֙ הַ⁠צֹּ֣לֵעָ֔ה וְ⁠הַ⁠נִּדָּחָ֖ה אֲקַבֵּ֑צָה

"I shall assemble the lame and gather the outcast"

Yahweh is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were a flock of sheep, some of them lame and some of them outcast, whom he gathers together. He is portraying himself as a shepherd who cares for his scattered and suffering people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I shall bring together my people who are weak and bring back those who were driven away]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 4:6 (#2)
content:
אֹֽסְפָה֙ הַ⁠צֹּ֣לֵעָ֔ה וְ⁠הַ⁠נִּדָּחָ֖ה אֲקַבֵּ֑צָה

"I shall assemble the lame and gather the outcast"

Yahweh is using the adjectives the lame and the outcast as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [I shall assemble those who are lame, and gather those who were outcast]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Micah 4:6 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠צֹּ֣לֵעָ֔ה וְ⁠הַ⁠נִּדָּחָ֖ה אֲקַבֵּ֑צָה

"the lame and gather the outcast"

Yahweh is using the adjectives the lame and the outcast as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the people who are lame and gather the people who have been cast out]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Micah 4:6 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֖ר הֲרֵעֹֽתִי

"and those whom I have afflicted"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will gather those whom I have afflicted]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 4:6 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֖ר הֲרֵעֹֽתִי

"and those whom I have afflicted"

Micah assumes that readers will know that those whom I have afflicted would refer to those who survived the previous judgment he predicted Yahweh would bring in the earlier portions. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in fact, I will gather all those who survive my discipline]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 4:7 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠שְׁאֵרִ֔ית

"into a remnant"

By remnant, Yahweh means those few people who he will allow to survive his discipline when he judges the sins of his people. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [into a people who will survive]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 4:7 (#2)
content:
יְהוָ֤ה

"Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person as modeled in the UST.

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Micah 4:8 (#1)
content:
מִגְדַּל־עֵ֗דֶר

"watchtower for the flock"

Yahweh is speaking of Jerusalem as if it were a watchtower from which a shepherd watches over his flock. He means that the city has the role of protecting and overseeing the people of God. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [protector of my people]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 4:8 (#2)
content:
בַּת־צִיּ֖וֹן

"daughter Zion"

Yahweh is using daughter Zion as a common expression of the culture to mean “the people of Jerusalem.” He refers to Jerusalem in the same way at the end of this verse. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Jerusalem]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 4:8 (#3)
content:
עָדֶ֣י⁠ךָ תֵּאתֶ֑ה וּ⁠בָאָ֗ה הַ⁠מֶּמְשָׁלָה֙ הָ⁠רִ֣אשֹׁנָ֔ה

"to you it will arrive, and the former dominion will come"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way as in the UST. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word other than and in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [your former dominion will come, indeed to you it will arrive]

See: Parallelism

title: Micah 4:8 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠מֶּמְשָׁלָה֙ הָ⁠רִ֣אשֹׁנָ֔ה

"the former dominion"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of dominion, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the right to rule as before]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 4:9 (#1)
content:
לָ֥⁠מָּה תָרִ֖יעִי רֵ֑עַ

"why do you shout a shout"

Micah is using the question form to challenge the people of Jerusalem about their loud crying. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [you are shouting loudly!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 4:9 (#2)
content:
תָרִ֖יעִי רֵ֑עַ

"do you shout a shout"

Micah is repeating forms of the verb shout in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [are you crying out so loudly]

See: Reduplication

title: Micah 4:9 (#3)
content:
הֲ⁠מֶ֣לֶךְ אֵֽין־בָּ֗⁠ךְ אִֽם־יוֹעֲצֵ⁠ךְ֙ אָבָ֔ד כִּֽי־הֶחֱזִיקֵ֥⁠ךְ חִ֖יל כַּ⁠יּוֹלֵדָֽה

"Is there no king among you, or has your counselor perished, that pain grips you like a woman giving birth"
