Micah is using the question form to prompt the people to recognize that they still have a king and a counselor to guide them and thus should not be crying out. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Since you have a king among you, and your counselor has not perished, you do not need to cry out like you are in as much pain as a woman giving birth.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 4:9 (#4)
content:
הֶחֱזִיקֵ֥⁠ךְ חִ֖יל כַּ⁠יּוֹלֵדָֽה

"pain grips you like a woman giving birth"

The point of this comparison is that just as a woman giving birth suffers severe pain, so the people of Jerusalem will experience the same intense anguish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [pain grips you as severely as the pain of a woman in labor]

See: Simile

title: Micah 4:9 (#5)
content:
חִ֖יל

"pain"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of pain, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [painful spasms]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 4:10 (#1)
content:
ח֧וּלִי וָ⁠גֹ֛חִי בַּת־צִיּ֖וֹן כַּ⁠יּֽוֹלֵדָ֑ה

"Writhe in pain and burst forth, daughter Zion, like a woman giving birth"

The point of this comparison is that just as a woman giving birth cries out and writhes in labor, so the people of Jerusalem will agonize in their distress. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Writhe in pain and cry out, people of Jerusalem, with the same intense anguish that a woman experiences when she is giving birth]

See: Simile

title: Micah 4:10 (#2)
content:
תִּנָּצֵ֔לִי

"you will be rescued"

The expression you will be rescued is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will be the one who rescues you]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 4:10 (#3)
content:
יְהוָ֔ה

"Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Micah 4:10 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠כַּ֖ף אֹיְבָֽיִ⁠ךְ

"from the hand of your enemies"

Here, the hand of their enemies represents their power and control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the power of your enemies]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 4:11 (#1)
content:
נֶאֶסְפ֥וּ עָלַ֖יִ⁠ךְ גּוֹיִ֣ם רַבִּ֑ים

"many nations are assembled against you"

The expression are assembled is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [many nations have gathered together against you]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 4:11 (#2)
content:
תֶּחֱנָ֔ף וְ⁠תַ֥חַז & עֵינֵֽי⁠נוּ

"Let her be defiled and let our eyes gaze"

The people of the other nations are saying what they want to happen to Jerusalem. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speakers will express in this context what they want to happen. Alternate translation: [We want her to be defiled and we want our eyes to gaze]

See: Third-Person Imperatives

title: Micah 4:11 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠תַ֥חַז בְּ⁠צִיּ֖וֹן עֵינֵֽי⁠נוּ

"and let our eyes gaze on Zion"

The nations are using the expression our eyes gaze as a common expression of the culture to mean “we will gloat over.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we want to look with satisfaction on Zion’s downfall]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 4:12 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֵ֗מָּה לֹ֤א יָֽדְעוּ֙

"But they, they do not know"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun they separately, even though the verb translated as they do not know already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize how ignorant the people of the other nations are of his thoughts. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But of course, they do not know]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 4:12 (#2)
content:
מַחְשְׁב֣וֹת יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א הֵבִ֖ינוּ עֲצָת֑⁠וֹ כִּ֥י קִבְּצָ֖⁠ם

"the thoughts of Yahweh and they do not understand his plan, for he has gathered them"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh, his, and he. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person here and throughout this verse. Alternate translation: [my thoughts and they do not understand my plan, for I have gather them]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Micah 4:12 (#3)
content:
מַחְשְׁב֣וֹת יְהוָ֔ה

"the thoughts of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of thoughts, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh intends]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 4:12 (#4)
content:
קִבְּצָ֖⁠ם כֶּ⁠עָמִ֥יר גֹּֽרְנָ⁠ה

"he has gathered them like bundles of grain for the threshing floor"

The point of this comparison is that just as bundles of grain are gathered to the threshing floor to be crushed, so Yahweh has gathered the nations together for judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he has gathered them together so that he can destroy them, just as a farmer gathers bundles of grain to the threshing floor to be crushed]

See: Simile

title: Micah 4:13 (#1)
content:
ק֧וּמִי וָ⁠ד֣וֹשִׁי בַת־צִיּ֗וֹן

"Arise and thresh, daughter Zion"

Yahweh is speaking of the people of Jerusalem, or daughter Zion, defeating her enemies as if she were an ox that could thresh grain. He means that Jerusalem will crush the nations as an ox crushes grain on the threshing floor. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Arise and crush your enemies, people of Jerusalem]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 4:13 (#2)
content:
קַרְנֵ֞⁠ךְ אָשִׂ֤ים בַּרְזֶל֙ וּ⁠פַרְסֹתַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ אָשִׂ֣ים נְחוּשָׁ֔ה

"I will make your horn iron, and I will make your hooves bronze"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way as in the UST. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word other than and in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [I will make your horn iron, indeed I will make your hooves bronze]

See: Parallelism

title: Micah 4:13 (#3)
content:
קַרְנֵ֞⁠ךְ אָשִׂ֤ים בַּרְזֶל֙

"I will make your horn iron"

Yahweh is speaking of the strength he will give Zion as if it were a horn made of iron. An animal’s horn represents power, and iron represents strength that cannot be broken. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will make you unbreakably strong]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 4:13 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠פַרְסֹתַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ אָשִׂ֣ים נְחוּשָׁ֔ה

"and I will make your hooves bronze"

Yahweh continues to speak of Zion as if it were a powerful threshing ox whose hooves he would make of bronze. He means that he will make Zion strong enough to trample and crush her enemies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will make you strong enough to trample your enemies]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 4:13 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הַחֲרַמְתִּ֤י לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ בִּצְעָ֔⁠ם וְ⁠חֵילָ֖⁠ם

"and devote to Yahweh their plunder and their wealth"

By devote, Yahweh means something that is irrevocably dedicated to him so that it cannot be taken back or used for any other purpose. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and permanently dedicate to Yahweh their plunder and their wealth]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 4:13 (#6)
content:
לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙

"to Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as to Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person as in the UST.

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Micah 4:13 (#7)
content:
בִּצְעָ֔⁠ם וְ⁠חֵילָ֖⁠ם

"their plunder and their wealth"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of plunder and wealth, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [what they have seized and what they own]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 4:13 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠חֵילָ֖⁠ם לַ⁠אֲד֥וֹן כָּל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"and their wealth to the Lord of all of the earth"

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and devote their wealth to the Lord of all of the earth]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah - Chapter 5 Introduction
content:
Micah 5 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Yahweh promises a ruler who will shepherd and deliver his people.

  1. Yahweh raises up a ruler from Bethlehem (1–6)
  2. Yahweh preserves his people among the nations (7–9)
  3. Yahweh removes all sources of false security and idolatry (10–15)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Messiah

This chapter contains a prophecy explaining that the Messiah was to be born in Bethlehem. This prophecy is fulfilled by Jesus’s birth and referenced in the New Testament in each of the gospel accounts of that event.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Change in Personal Pronouns

Extra care must be taken in translating pronouns in this chapter. Sometimes “I” is a reference to the author and other times it is a reference to Yahweh. There is also a noticeable shift where the author stops speaking about the people as “you” and begins speaking about them as “we” or “us.”

title: Micah 5:1 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠שֵּׁ֨בֶט֙ יַכּ֣וּ עַֽל־הַ⁠לְּחִ֔י

"with the rod they strike on the cheek"

Micah is using with the rod they strike on the cheek as a common expression of the culture to mean “they insult and humiliate him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they utterly humiliate]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 5:1 (#2)
content:
בַת־גְּד֔וּד

"daughter troop"

Micah is speaking of the surviving remnant of the people of Jerusalem (whom he previously called “daughter Zion”) as if they were a daughter troop. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

title: Micah 5:1 (#3)
content:
מָצ֖וֹר שָׂ֣ם עָלֵ֑י⁠נוּ

"He has set a siege against us"

The pronoun He refers to the enemy who is attacking Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Our enemy has laid siege against us]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:1 (#4)
content:
עָלֵ֑י⁠נוּ

"against us"

By us, Micah means himself and the people of Jerusalem to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Micah 5:2 (#1)
content:
בֵּֽית־לֶ֣חֶם אֶפְרָ֗תָה

"Bethlehem Ephrathah"

Bethlehem Ephrathah is the name of a town located in a region of Judah (see it referenced in Matthew 2:6). Ephrathah distinguished it from another town called “Bethlehem” in the region of Zebulun. It is also called “the city of David” in Luke 2:4, since it was where David, king of Israel, was born.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Micah 5:2 (#2)
content:
מִמְּ⁠ךָ֙ לִ֣⁠י יֵצֵ֔א

"from you will come out for me"

The pronoun me refers to Yahweh, who is speaking these words through Micah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from you will come out for Yahweh]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:2 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠מוֹצָאֹתָ֥י⁠ו מִ⁠קֶּ֖דֶם

"and his goings out {are} from aforetime"

Micah is using his goings out as a common expression of the culture to mean “his origin.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his origin is from ancient times]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 5:2 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠ימֵ֥י עוֹלָֽם

"from the days of eternity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of eternity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the days before time began]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 5:3 (#1)
content:
יִתְּנֵ֔⁠ם

"he will give them up"

The pronoun he refers to Yahweh, and the pronoun them refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will give the people of Israel up]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:3 (#2)
content:
עַד־עֵ֥ת יוֹלֵדָ֖ה יָלָ֑דָה

"until the time {when} the bearing {one} gives birth"

This prophecy appears to have two fulfillments. The first fulfillment would be when God brings the people of Israel back to their land. In this case, the bearing one would refer to “daughter Zion” 4:10, who stands for the faithful remnant of Israel. She gives birth to the restored nation of Israel. The second and greater fulfillment is when the mother of the Messiah gives birth to him who is able to create the new, fully restored people of God, bringing together the remnant of Israel and all of his brothers redeemed from the rest of mankind. If possible, translate this in a way that can apply to both fulfillments.

title: Micah 5:3 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יֶ֣תֶר אֶחָ֔י⁠ו

"and the remainder of his brothers"

The pronoun his refers to the ruler whom Yahweh has promised. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the remainder of that ruler’s brothers]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:3 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יֶ֣תֶר אֶחָ֔י⁠ו

"and the remainder of his brothers"

Micah is speaking of the fellow Israelites of this ruler as if they were his brothers. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the remainder of his fellow Israelites]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 5:4 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עָמַ֗ד

"And he will stand"

The pronoun he refers to the ruler that Yahweh promised to raise up from Bethlehem, whom Micah described in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the ruler will stand]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:4 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עָמַ֗ד וְ⁠רָעָה֙

"And he will stand and shepherd"

Micah is speaking of this ruler as if he would shepherd as one who cares for a flock of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will take his stand and lead and provide for his people]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 5:4 (#3)
content:
בִּ⁠גְא֕וֹן שֵׁ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהָ֑י⁠ו

"in the majesty of the name of Yahweh his God"

Here, the name of Yahweh represents Yahweh himself and his authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the majestic authority of Yahweh his God]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 5:4 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יָשָׁ֕בוּ

"And they will dwell"

The pronoun they refers to the people of Israel, whom this ruler will shepherd. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the people of Israel will live securely]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:5 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֥ה זֶ֖ה שָׁל֑וֹם

"And this one will be peace"

Micah is speaking of this ruler bringing peace as if he were peace itself. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And this one will bring peace to his people]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 5:5 (#2)
content:
יָב֣וֹא

"he comes"

The personal pronouns he and him throughout this verse refer to Assyria, which stands for the Assyrian army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Assyria—when the Assyrian army comes into our land]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:5 (#3)
content:
בְ⁠אַרְצֵ֗⁠נוּ וְ⁠כִ֤י יִדְרֹךְ֙ בְּ⁠אַרְמְנֹתֵ֔י⁠נוּ

"into our land, and when he treads on our citadels"

By our and we, Micah means himself and the people of Israel to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Micah 5:5 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠הֲקֵמֹ֤נוּ עָלָי⁠ו֙

"then we will raise up against him"

Micah is speaking of the people choosing leaders as if they would raise up these leaders to a high place. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then we will choose to fight against them]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 5:5 (#5)
content:
שִׁבְעָ֣ה רֹעִ֔ים וּ⁠שְׁמֹנָ֖ה נְסִיכֵ֥י אָדָֽם

"seven shepherds and eight princes of man"

Micah is using seven shepherds and eight princes of man as a common expression of the culture to mean “as many leaders as will be needed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as many leaders as will be needed]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 5:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠רָע֞וּ

"And they will shepherd"

The pronoun they refers to the leaders mentioned in the previous verse who will fight against Assyria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And these leaders will shepherd]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:6 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠רָע֞וּ אֶת־אֶ֤רֶץ אַשּׁוּר֙ בַּ⁠חֶ֔רֶב

"And they will shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword"

Micah is speaking of these leaders ruling with military power as if they would shepherd them like a herd of sheep but in this context of the Assyrians, it would be with a sword. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they will rule the land of Assyria with military power]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 5:6 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אֶת־אֶ֥רֶץ נִמְרֹ֖ד בִּ⁠פְתָחֶ֑י⁠הָ

"and the land of Nimrod in its entrances"

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will shepherd the land of Nimrod in its entrances]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 5:6 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אֶת־אֶ֥רֶץ נִמְרֹ֖ד

"and the land of Nimrod"

Here, the land of Nimrod represents the territory that the ancient ruler Nimrod founded, that is, Assyria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [which is the land that Nimrod founded,]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Micah 5:6 (#5)
content:
בִּ⁠פְתָחֶ֑י⁠הָ

"in its entrances"

The phrase in its entrances is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that the original reading was a very similar word meaning “drawn sword,” which is represented in some ancient translations. You may want to follow this reading, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [with a drawn sword]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Micah 5:6 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠הִצִּיל֙ מֵֽ⁠אַשּׁ֔וּר

"And he will deliver {us} from Assyria"

The pronoun he refers to the ruler whom Yahweh has promised. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the promised ruler will rescue us from Assyria]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:7 (#1)
content:
שְׁאֵרִ֣ית יַעֲקֹ֗ב

"the remnant of Jacob"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of remnant, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those of Jacob who remain]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 5:7 (#2)
content:
שְׁאֵרִ֣ית יַעֲקֹ֗ב

"the remnant of Jacob"

Here, Jacob represents the descendants of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the remnant of the people of Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 5:7 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠טַל֙ מֵ⁠אֵ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה כִּ⁠רְבִיבִ֖ים עֲלֵי־עֵ֑שֶׂב

"like dew from Yahweh, like showers on the grass"

The point of this comparison is that just as dew and showers come from Yahweh and refresh the grass, so the survivors of Israel will be a blessing to the many peoples among whom they live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [a blessing to them, like refreshing dew that comes from Yahweh, like showers on the grass]

See: Simile

title: Micah 5:7 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־יְקַוֶּה֙ לְ⁠אִ֔ישׁ

"that does not wait for a man"

The pronoun that refers to the dew and the showers, which come from Yahweh rather than from any human effort. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [moisture that does not wait for a man]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:7 (#5)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־יְקַוֶּה֙ לְ⁠אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠לֹ֥א יְיַחֵ֖ל לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י אָדָֽם

"that does not wait for a man and does not hope for the sons of man"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [that does depend completely on Yahweh and not on people at all]

See: Parallelism

title: Micah 5:7 (#6)
content:
לֹֽא־יְקַוֶּה֙ לְ⁠אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠לֹ֥א יְיַחֵ֖ל לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י אָדָֽם

"does not wait for a man and does not hope for the sons of man"

Here, a man and the sons of man represent people in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [does not wait for anyone and does not hope for any human being]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Micah 5:8 (#1)
content:
שְׁאֵרִ֨ית יַעֲקֹ֜ב

"the remnant of Jacob"

See how you translated the abstract noun remnant in 5:7.

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 5:8 (#2)
content:
שְׁאֵרִ֨ית יַעֲקֹ֜ב

"the remnant of Jacob"

See how you translated Jacob in 5:7.

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 5:8 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠אַרְיֵה֙ בְּ⁠בַהֲמ֣וֹת יַ֔עַר כִּ⁠כְפִ֖יר בְּ⁠עֶדְרֵי צֹ֑אן

"like a lion among the animals of the forest, like a young lion among the flocks of sheep"

The point of this comparison is that just as a lion is stronger than the other animals and a young lion can attack a flock of sheep without being stopped, so the survivors of Israel will be stronger than the peoples among whom they live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as strong as a lion among the animals of the forest, as unstoppable as a young lion among the flocks of sheep]

See: Simile

title: Micah 5:8 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠רָמַ֥ס וְ⁠טָרַ֖ף

"both tramples and tears"

The terms tramples and tears mean similar things. Micah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [tears to pieces]

See: Doublet

title: Micah 5:9 (#1)
content:
תָּרֹ֥ם יָדְ⁠ךָ֖ עַל־צָרֶ֑י⁠ךָ וְ⁠כָל־אֹיְבֶ֖י⁠ךָ יִכָּרֵֽתוּ

"May your hand rise over your adversaries, and may all of your enemies be cut off"

Some ancient manuscripts read according to the ULT. Other ancient manuscripts read “Your hand will rise over your adversaries, and all of your enemies will be cut off.” In that case, “your” could refer either to Yahweh or to Jacob, who represents his descendants. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

See: Textual Variants

title: Micah 5:9 (#2)
content:
תָּרֹ֥ם יָדְ⁠ךָ֖ עַל־צָרֶ֑י⁠ךָ וְ⁠כָל־אֹיְבֶ֖י⁠ךָ יִכָּרֵֽתוּ

"May your hand rise over your adversaries, and may all of your enemies be cut off"

Micah is saying what he wants Yahweh to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, I desire that your hand rise over your adversaries and that all your enemies be destroyed]

See: Third-Person Imperatives

title: Micah 5:9 (#3)
content:
תָּרֹ֥ם יָדְ⁠ךָ֖ עַל־צָרֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"May your hand rise over your adversaries"

Here, your hand represents Yahweh’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [May you triumph by your power over your adversaries]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 5:9 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־אֹיְבֶ֖י⁠ךָ יִכָּרֵֽתוּ

"and may all of your enemies be cut off"

The expression be cut off is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and may you cut off all of your enemies]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 5:9 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־אֹיְבֶ֖י⁠ךָ יִכָּרֵֽתוּ

"and may all of your enemies be cut off"

Micah is using be cut off as a common expression of the culture to mean “be destroyed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may all of your enemies be destroyed]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 5:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֤ה בַ⁠יּוֹם־הַ⁠הוּא֙

"And it will be on that day"

Micah is using on that day as a common expression of the culture to mean “at that time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it will be when that happens]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Micah 5:10 (#2)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

Micah is using the declaration of Yahweh to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Micah 5:10 (#3)
content:
סוּסֶ֖י⁠ךָ מִ⁠קִּרְבֶּ֑⁠ךָ וְ⁠הַאֲבַדְתִּ֖י מַרְכְּבֹתֶֽי⁠ךָ

"your horses from your midst, and I will destroy your chariots"

Here, horses and chariots represent “military power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your military power and I will destroy your means of waging war]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 5:10 (#4)
content:
סוּסֶ֖י⁠ךָ מִ⁠קִּרְבֶּ֑⁠ךָ

"your horses from your midst"

The pronoun your refers to the people of Israel, whom Yahweh is addressing here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your horses from your midst, people of Israel]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 5:11 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּ֖י

"And I will cut off"

Yahweh is using cut off as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will destroy]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 5:12 (#1)
content:
כְשָׁפִ֖ים מִ⁠יָּדֶ֑⁠ךָ

"sorceries from your hand"

Here, your hand represents “what you do.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [sorceries from what you do]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 5:12 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּ֥י כְשָׁפִ֖ים מִ⁠יָּדֶ֑⁠ךָ

"And I will cut off sorceries from your hand"

Yahweh is using cut off to mean “destroy” and sorceries from your hand to represent their power to practice witchcraft. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will destroy your power to practice sorcery]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 5:12 (#3)
content:
כְשָׁפִ֖ים

"sorceries"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of sorceries, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the practice of magic]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 5:12 (#4)
content:
לֹ֥א יִֽהְיוּ־לָֽ⁠ךְ

"will not be to you"

Yahweh is using be to you as a common expression of the culture to mean “you will no longer have.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will no longer have]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 5:13 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּ֧י

"And I will cut off"

Yahweh is using cut off as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy completely” or “get rid of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will wipe out] or [And I will get rid of]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 5:13 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֥ה ע֖וֹד

"and you will & longer"

To bow down was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and submission. In this context, it was an action by which a person showed worship or submission to an idol. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and you will not submit yourselves]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Micah 5:13 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יָדֶֽי⁠ךָ

"to the work of your hands"

Yahweh is using the work of your hands to represent the things that the people make and do, particularly idols and acts of worship directed toward them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the idols you make and worship]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 5:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַשְׁתִּ֥י אֲשֵׁירֶ֖י⁠ךָ

"And I will uproot your Asherah s"

Yahweh is speaking of the poles that the people use to worship the goddess Asherah as if they were plants that he would uproot. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will tear out your Asherah poles]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 5:15 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠אַ֧ף

"in nose"

Yahweh is using in nose as a common expression of the culture to mean “in anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in anger]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 5:15 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠אַ֧ף וּ⁠בְ⁠חֵמָ֛ה

"in nose and in wrath"

The terms nose and wrath mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [in furious anger]

See: Doublet

title: Micah 5:15 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠חֵמָ֛ה נָקָ֖ם

"and in wrath vengeance"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of vengeance, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and in wrath I will avenge myself]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 5:15 (#4)
content:
לֹ֥א שָׁמֵֽעוּ

"have not listened"

Yahweh assumes that readers will know that listened as it is used here, includes the meaning of “obeyed.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers as modeled in the UST.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah - Chapter 6 Introduction
content:
Micah 6 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written as a court case or lawsuit by Yahweh against His people. Yahweh calls his people to repentance and faithful living.

  1. Yahweh brings his case against Israel (1–5)
  2. Yahweh desires justice, mercy, and humble obedience (6–8)
  3. Yahweh announces judgment for Israel’s sin (9–16)

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Names in lawsuit

Moses, Aaron and Miriam are mentioned as witnesses for Yahweh and against Israel.

title: Micah 6:1 (#1)
content:
ק֚וּם רִ֣יב אֶת־הֶ⁠הָרִ֔ים וְ⁠תִשְׁמַ֥עְנָה הַ⁠גְּבָע֖וֹת קוֹלֶֽ⁠ךָ

"Arise, contend before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh commands me to arise and contend before the mountains, and to let the hills hear my voice]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Micah 6:1 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠תִשְׁמַ֥עְנָה הַ⁠גְּבָע֖וֹת

"and let the hills hear"

Yahweh is saying what he wants the hills to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants to happen. Alternate translation: [the hills should be able to hear]

See: Third-Person Imperatives

title: Micah 6:1 (#3)
content:
קוֹלֶֽ⁠ךָ

"your voice"

The pronoun your refers to Micah, the prophet whom Yahweh is commanding to speak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your voice, Micah]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:2 (#1)
content:
שִׁמְע֤וּ הָרִים֙ אֶת־רִ֣יב יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠הָ⁠אֵתָנִ֖ים מֹ֣סְדֵי אָ֑רֶץ

"Hear the dispute of Yahweh, mountains, and permanent foundations of the earth"

Micah is speaking to the mountains and the foundations of the earth, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about everything in all creation hearing the case that Yahweh is bringing against them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the mountains and the foundations of the earth. Alternate translation: [Let all creation hear the dispute of Yahweh]

See: Apostrophe

title: Micah 6:2 (#2)
content:
אֶת־רִ֣יב יְהוָ֔ה

"the dispute of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of dispute, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh as he disputes]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:2 (#3)
content:
עִם־עַמּ֔⁠וֹ

"with his people"

The pronoun his refers to Yahweh, and the phrase his people refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [with the Israelites, his people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:2 (#4)
content:
כִּ֣י רִ֤יב לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ עִם־עַמּ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠עִם־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל יִתְוַכָּֽח

"for a dispute{is} to Yahweh with his people, and with Israel he will argue"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [for Yahweh has a dispute that he is bringing against his people, Israel]

See: Parallelism

title: Micah 6:2 (#5)
content:
רִ֤יב לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ עִם־עַמּ֔⁠וֹ

"a dispute{is} to Yahweh with his people"

Micah is using a dispute is to Yahweh as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh has a dispute.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has a dispute with his people]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 6:3 (#1)
content:
עַמִּ֛⁠י מֶה־עָשִׂ֥יתִי לְ⁠ךָ֖

"My people, what have I done to you"

This verse begins a direct quotation from Yahweh that continues through verse 5. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh as modeled in the UST.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Micah 6:3 (#2)
content:
מֶה־עָשִׂ֥יתִי לְ⁠ךָ֖ וּ⁠מָ֣ה הֶלְאֵתִ֑י⁠ךָ

"what have I done to you, and how have I wearied you"

Yahweh is using the question form to assert that he has done nothing to harm his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have done nothing to harm you or to burden you!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 6:3 (#3)
content:
עֲנֵ֥ה בִּֽ⁠י

"Testify against me"

By Testify against me, Yahweh is using the language of a court and saying that if they actually have anything to accuse him of, they should testify. The implication from the previous questions is that they have nothing to accuse him of. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Only if I have done anything wrong can you testify against me]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 6:4 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִ⁠בֵּ֥ית עֲבָדִ֖ים

"and from the house of slaves"

Yahweh is speaking of Egypt as if it had been a house where people kept slaves. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and from where you were held as slaves]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 6:4 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠פָנֶ֔י⁠ךָ

"to your face"

Here, to your face represents “before you” or “ahead of you.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [ahead of you]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 6:5 (#1)
content:
זְכָר & מַה־יָּעַ֗ץ בָּלָק֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ מוֹאָ֔ב וּ⁠מֶה־עָנָ֥ה אֹת֖⁠וֹ בִּלְעָ֣ם בֶּן־בְּע֑וֹר

"remember what Balak, king of Moab, counseled, and what Balaam, son of Beor, answered him"

Yahweh assumes that readers will know that he is referring to the events describe in Numbers 22–24. The phrase what Balak, king of Moab, counseled refers to his plot to destroy Israel by hiring Balaam to curse them and what Balaam, son of Beor, answered him refers to the fact that Balaam told the king he could only bless the people rather than curse them. You could include this information in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 6:5 (#2)
content:
מִן־הַ⁠שִּׁטִּים֙ עַד־הַ⁠גִּלְגָּ֔ל

"from Shittim to Gilgal"

The implication is that Yahweh wants his people to remember what happened to their ancestors when they were able to miraculously cross the Jordan River (see Joshua 3 and 4). Shittim was the location of their last camp east of the Jordan River, and Gilgal, was where first camped in the land that he had promised them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and remember what I did for your ancestors when they crossed the Jordan River]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Micah 6:5 (#3)
content:
צִדְק֥וֹת יְהוָֽה

"the righteousnesses of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of righteousnesses, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how Yahweh acted righteously toward you]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:6 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠מָּה֙ אֲקַדֵּ֣ם יְהוָ֔ה

"With what shall I come before Yahweh"

This verse begins a shift from Yahweh’s words to the direct quotation spoken by a worshiper who represents the people. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating this shift in speaker.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Micah 6:6 (#2)
content:
אִכַּ֖ף לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֣י

"bow down to the God of"

To bow down was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and worship. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [worship the God of]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Micah 6:6 (#3)
content:
אִכַּ֖ף

"bow down"

The speaker is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [With what shall I bow down]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 6:6 (#4)
content:
לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֣י מָר֑וֹם

"to the God of the height"

The speaker is using the possessive form to describe a God that is characterized by the height, that is, by his exalted position. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the exalted God]

See: Possession

title: Micah 6:6 (#5)
content:
בַּ⁠עֲגָלִ֖ים בְּנֵ֥י שָׁנָֽה

"with calves, sons of a year"

The speaker is using calves, sons of a year as a common expression of the culture to mean “calves that are one year old.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with calves that are one year old]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 6:7 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠אַלְפֵ֣י אֵילִ֔ים בְּ⁠רִֽבְב֖וֹת נַֽחֲלֵי־שָׁ֑מֶן

"with thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil"

The speaker says thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [an enormous number of rams, with an unimaginable amount of oil]

See: Hyperbole

title: Micah 6:7 (#2)
content:
פִּשְׁעִ֔⁠י

"for} my transgression"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of transgression, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the ways I have rebelled]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:7 (#3)
content:
פְּרִ֥י בִטְנִ֖⁠י

"the fruit of my belly"

Here the speaker is speaking of a child who came from his own body as if it were the fruit of my belly. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my own child that I fathered]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 6:8 (#1)
content:
הִגִּ֥יד לְ⁠ךָ֛ אָדָ֖ם

"He has told you, man"

In this verse the speaker changes, as Micah answers the questions that the previous speaker has asked. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating a change of speaker in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Micah 6:8 (#2)
content:
הִגִּ֥יד

"He has told"

The pronoun He refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has told]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:8 (#3)
content:
אָדָ֖ם

"man"

Micah is not referring to a specific man. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [human being]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Micah 6:8 (#4)
content:
מִשְׁפָּט֙

"justice"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of justice, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is right and fair]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:8 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אַ֣הֲבַת חֶ֔סֶד

"and the love of covenant faithfulness"

Micah is using the possessive form to describe a love that is characterized as covenant faithfulness. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and love faithfully]

See: Possession

title: Micah 6:8 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠אַ֣הֲבַת חֶ֔סֶד

"and the love of covenant faithfulness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of covenant faithfulness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and faithfully loving others]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:8 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠הַצְנֵ֥עַ לֶ֖כֶת עִם־אֱלֹהֶֽי⁠ךָ

"and to be humble to walk with your God"

Here Micah is speaking of how one lives as if it were to walk down a path and by with your God, he means that one should live one’s whole life in fellowship with God. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to be humble as you live your whole life in fellowship with your God]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 6:8 (#8)
content:
אֱלֹהֶֽי⁠ךָ

"your God"

Micah is using the possessive form your God to mean that Yahweh is the God whom the people worship, not that they possess or control him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom you worship]

See: Possession

title: Micah 6:9 (#1)
content:
ק֤וֹל יְהוָה֙ & יִקְרָ֔א

"The voice of Yahweh calls"

The phrase The voice of Yahweh represents the message that Yahweh speaks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The message that Yahweh speaks]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 6:9 (#2)
content:
לָ⁠עִ֣יר

"to the city"

Here, the city represents the people who live in the city of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of the city]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 6:9 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠תוּשִׁיָּ֖ה יִרְאֶ֣ה שְׁמֶ֑⁠ךָ

"and sound wisdom fears your name"

Micah has been speaking to the people about Yahweh, but here he briefly turns aside and addresses Yahweh directly. He does this in order to express more powerfully his own reverence for Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could introduce this more clearly and put the rest of this address in quote marks. Alternate translation: [and I say to Yahweh, “Sound wisdom fears your name”]

See: Aside

title: Micah 6:9 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠תוּשִׁיָּ֖ה

"and sound wisdom"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of sound wisdom, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and whoever is truly wise]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:9 (#5)
content:
שְׁמֶ֑⁠ךָ

"your name"

Here, your name represents Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you yourself]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 6:9 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠מִ֥י יְעָדָֽ⁠הּ

"and whoever he appointed"

The pronoun he refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and whoever Yahweh appointed]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:9 (#7)
content:
וּ⁠מִ֥י יְעָדָֽ⁠הּ

"and whoever he appointed"

The phrase and whoever he appointed is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Scholars have proposed, however, that the first word of the next verse should actually belong to this verse, and that the letters of the words have been divided incorrectly in the present text. By adding the first word of verse 10 to this phrase, changing two letters in it, and dividing the words differently, the meaning would be as in this alternate translation. You may want to follow the ULT or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and the assembly of the city]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Micah 6:10 (#1)
content:
ע֗וֹד הַ⁠אִשׁ֙ בֵּ֣ית רָשָׁ֔ע אֹצְר֖וֹת רֶ֑שַׁע וְ⁠אֵיפַ֥ת רָז֖וֹן זְעוּמָֽה

"Are there still {in} the house of the wicked treasuries of wickedness, and the ephah of leanness {that is} cursed"

Yahweh is using the question form to accuse the people of the city of cheating others in their business dealings. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There are still in the house of the wicked treasuries of wickedness, and the ephah of leanness that is cursed!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 6:10 (#2)
content:
ע֗וֹד הַ⁠אִשׁ֙

"Are there still"

The phrase Are there still is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. The wording in the text, however, is very unusual, and scholars have proposed that the first word should be read with the previous verse and that a letter has dropped off of the second word. Reading the text in this way results in the following alternate translation. You may want to follow the ULT or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [Can I forget]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Micah 6:10 (#3)
content:
רָשָׁ֔ע

"the wicked"

Yahweh is using the adjective wicked as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the person who is wicked]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Micah 6:10 (#4)
content:
רֶ֑שַׁע

"wickedness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wickedness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [things gained wickedly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:10 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אֵיפַ֥ת רָז֖וֹן

"and the ephah of leanness"

This ephah was equivalent to 22 liters or nearly two thirds of a bushel. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this in terms of modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote.

See: Biblical Volume

title: Micah 6:10 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠אֵיפַ֥ת רָז֖וֹן

"and the ephah of leanness"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe an ephah that is characterized by leanness, that is, a measure that holds less than it should. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the undersized ephah]

See: Possession

title: Micah 6:10 (#7)
content:
זְעוּמָֽה

"that is} cursed"

The expression is cursed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that I, Yahweh, have cursed]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 6:11 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠אֶזְכֶּ֖ה בְּ⁠מֹ֣אזְנֵי רֶ֑שַׁע וּ⁠בְ⁠כִ֖יס אַבְנֵ֥י מִרְמָֽה

"Would I be innocent with scales of wickedness, and with a bag of stones of deceit"

Yahweh is using the question form to declare that no one who uses dishonest weights and measures can be innocent. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I certainly would not be innocent if I used scales of wickedness and a bag of stones of deceit!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Micah 6:11 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠אֶזְכֶּ֖ה

"Would I be innocent"

The phrase Would I be innocent is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. It would also be possible to read the word as “Would I acquit.” You may want to follow the ULT or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [Would I acquit someone]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Micah 6:11 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠מֹ֣אזְנֵי רֶ֑שַׁע

"with scales of wickedness"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe scales that are used for wickedness or cheating people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with unjust scales]

See: Possession

title: Micah 6:11 (#4)
content:
אַבְנֵ֥י מִרְמָֽה

"stones of deceit"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe stones, which were used to weigh things they were selling, that are characterized by deceit because they were the wrong weight. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [deceitful stones]

See: Possession

title: Micah 6:12 (#1)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֤ר עֲשִׁירֶ֨י⁠הָ֙

"which her rich"

The words which and her refer to the city that Yahweh mentioned in verse 9. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [—the city whose rich]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:12 (#2)
content:
עֲשִׁירֶ֨י⁠הָ֙

"her rich"

Yahweh is using the adjective rich as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [her rich people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Micah 6:12 (#3)
content:
חָמָ֔ס

"violence"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of violence, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent acts]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:12 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יֹשְׁבֶ֖י⁠הָ דִּבְּרוּ־שָׁ֑קֶר וּ⁠לְשׁוֹנָ֖⁠ם רְמִיָּ֥ה בְּ⁠פִי⁠הֶֽם

"and her inhabitants speak falsehood, and their tongue {is} deceit in their mouth"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. You could use the approach which is modeled in the UST of connecting the phrases with a word other than “and” that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Another approach would be to combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and all her inhabitants speak deceitfully]

See: Parallelism

title: Micah 6:12 (#5)
content:
שָׁ֑קֶר

"falsehood"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of falsehood, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [her inhabitants speak falsely]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:12 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠לְשׁוֹנָ֖⁠ם רְמִיָּ֥ה בְּ⁠פִי⁠הֶֽם

"and their tongue {is} deceit in their mouth"

Here, tongue represents speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and what they say is deceitful]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 6:13 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠גַם־אֲנִ֖י הֶחֱלֵ֣יתִי

"And even I, I will make sick"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I will make already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh himself is the one who will act. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And even I, myself will make sick]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:13 (#2)
content:
הֶחֱלֵ֣יתִי הַכּוֹתֶ֑⁠ךָ

"I will make sick the striking of you"

Yahweh is using make sick the striking of you as a common expression of the culture to mean that he will administer an incurable injury on them. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will strike you with an incurable wound]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 6:13 (#3)
content:
הַכּוֹתֶ֑⁠ךָ

"the striking of you"

The pronouns you and your from here to the end of the chapter refer to the people of the city of Jerusalem whom Yahweh is now addressing directly after speaking about them in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the striking of you, inhabitants of Jerusalem]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:14 (#1)
content:
אַתָּ֤ה תֹאכַל֙

"You, you will eat"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun you separately, even though the verb translated as you will eat already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between the heavenly Judge and the sentence they will suffer. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For your part, you will eat]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:14 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יֶשְׁחֲ⁠ךָ֖ בְּ⁠קִרְבֶּ֑⁠ךָ

"for dysentery {will be} inside you"

The word dysentery refers to a kind of disease of the bowels that empties the body of the food it takes in. If your readers would not be familiar with what dysentery is, you could use the name of a similar sickness that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [because your stomach will be empty]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Micah 6:14 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠תַסֵּג֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א תַפְלִ֔יט וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר תְּפַלֵּ֖ט

"And you will bring to safety but not deliver, and what you do deliver"

The word translated as bring to safety could also be the word for “reach.” This leads some scholars to interpret these sentences in the context of birthing rather than warfare. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [And you will reach birth, but not deliver the baby]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Micah 6:14 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠חֶ֥רֶב אֶתֵּֽן

"I will give to the sword"

Here, the sword represents warfare and being killed in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will hand over to be killed in war]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 6:15 (#1)
content:
אַתָּ֥ה תִזְרַ֖ע וְ⁠לֹ֣א תִקְצ֑וֹר אַתָּ֤ה תִדְרֹֽךְ

"You, you will sow but not reap; you, you will tread"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun you separately, even though the verbs translated as you will sow and you will tread already include this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize how the people will suffer. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You people of the city will certainly sow, but not reap, and you will certainly tread]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠תִיר֖וֹשׁ וְ⁠לֹ֥א תִשְׁתֶּה־יָּֽיִן

"and—new wine but not drink wine"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and you will tread new wine grapes but not drink wine]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 6:16 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יִשְׁתַּמֵּ֞ר חֻקּ֣וֹת עָמְרִ֗י

"For the statutes of Omri are kept"

The expression are kept is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For the people keep the statutes of Omri]

See: Active or Passive

title: Micah 6:16 (#2)
content:
חֻקּ֣וֹת עָמְרִ֗י

"the statutes of Omri"

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the statutes that Omri established. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the statutes that Omri established]

See: Possession

title: Micah 6:16 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠כֹל֙ מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה בֵית־אַחְאָ֔ב

"and all of the deeds of the house of Ahab"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and all of the deeds of the house of Ahab are kept]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 6:16 (#4)
content:
בֵית־אַחְאָ֔ב

"the house of Ahab"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Ahab figuratively means all the people descended from that evil king as modeled in the UST.

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 6:16 (#5)
content:
בֵית־אַחְאָ֔ב

"the house of Ahab"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the descendants of Ahab were a house. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Ahab]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 6:16 (#6)
content:
וַ⁠תֵּלְכ֖וּ בְּ⁠מֹֽעֲצוֹתָ֑⁠ם

"and you have walked in their counsels"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if living according to the advice of Omri and Ahab were to have walked in their counsels. He is referring to the corrupt policies, economic injustice, and foreign idol worship (like Baal worship) institutionalized by Omri and his son, Ahab (see 1 Kings 16). Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have followed their advice]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 6:16 (#7)
content:
לְ⁠שַׁמָּ֗ה

"a desolation"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of a desolation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [desolate]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 6:16 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠יֹשְׁבֶ֨י⁠הָ֙

"and her inhabitants"

The pronoun her refers to the city that Yahweh mentioned in verse 9. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the inhabitants of that city]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 6:16 (#9)
content:
לִ⁠שְׁרֵקָ֔ה

"a hissing"

Here, a hissing represents the scorn that people will express toward those who live in the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and her inhabitants an object of scorn]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah - Chapter 7 Introduction
content:
Micah 7 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Yahweh hears the repentant and faithfully restores his people

  1. Micah laments Israel’s corruption (1–6)
  2. Micah waits in hope for Yahweh’s salvation (7–13)
  3. Yahweh shows mercy and remains faithful to his covenant (14–20)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Last days

This chapter looks forward to the hope of the coming savior for the faithful remnant. This is the future restoration of Israel when true peace will come.

Prophet

The prophet was able to speak to God on behalf of the people. Often in this chapter, the prophet speaks in Israel’s place and offers repentance to Yahweh.

title: Micah 7:1 (#1)
content:
אַ֣לְלַי לִ֗⁠י

"Woe to me"

Micah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of distress. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How sorrowful I feel]

See: Exclamations

title: Micah 7:1 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠אָסְפֵּי־קַ֔יִץ כְּ⁠עֹלְלֹ֖ת בָּצִ֑יר

"like the gatherings of summer fruit, like the gleanings of the grape harvest"

The point of this comparison is that just as the gatherings of summer fruit and the gleanings of the grape harvest are what remains after everything worth having has already been taken, so is the land in which Micah is searching for a faithful person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like one searching where the summer fruit has already been gathered, like one searching where the grapes have already been harvested]

See: Simile

title: Micah 7:1 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠אָסְפֵּי־קַ֔יִץ

"like the gatherings of summer fruit"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of gatherings, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [trying to gather summer fruit after others have already picked all of it]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 7:1 (#4)
content:
כְּ⁠עֹלְלֹ֖ת בָּצִ֑יר

"like the gleanings of the grape harvest"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of gleanings, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like what is left over after others have harvested the grapes]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 7:1 (#5)
content:
נַפְשִֽׁ⁠י

"my soul desires"

Here, my soul represents Micah himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I desire]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 7:2 (#1)
content:
כֻּלָּ⁠ם֙ לְ⁠דָמִ֣ים יֶאֱרֹ֔בוּ

"All of them lie in wait for bloodshed"

Micah says All of them lie in wait for bloodshed as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Nearly everyone lies in wait for bloodshed]

See: Hyperbole

title: Micah 7:2 (#2)
content:
אָבַ֤ד חָסִיד֙

"The faithful one has perished"

Micah is not referring to a specific faithful one. He means faithful people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [All the faithful people have perished]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Micah 7:2 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יָשָׁ֥ר בָּ⁠אָדָ֖ם אָ֑יִן

"and there is no upright one among mankind"

Micah is not referring to a specific upright one. He means upright people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and there are no upright people among mankind]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Micah 7:2 (#4)
content:
כֻּלָּ⁠ם֙

"All of them"

The pronoun them refers to the people who live in the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [All of the people that are left in the land]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 7:2 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠דָמִ֣ים יֶאֱרֹ֔בוּ

"lie in wait for bloodshed"

Here, bloodshed represents violent death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [are just waiting to murder each other]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 7:2 (#6)
content:
אִ֥ישׁ אֶת־אָחִ֖י⁠הוּ יָצ֥וּדוּ חֵֽרֶם

"each man hunts his brother with a net"

Here Micah is speaking the people of the land exploiting each other as if they were trappers that are trying to catch an animal with a net. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each man seeks to trap his brother]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 7:2 (#7)
content:
אֶת־אָחִ֖י⁠הוּ

"his brother"

Micah is speaking as if a man’s brother, or fellow Israelite, were his prey, whom he hunts to harm rather than someone he should love and protect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each man tries to harm his fellow Israelite]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 7:3 (#1)
content:
הָ⁠רַ֤ע

"evil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of evil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [doing evil things]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 7:3 (#2)
content:
כַּפַּ֨יִם֙

"the two hands"

Here, the two hands represent the leaders who use them to do evil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [these leaders]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 7:3 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠שֹּׁפֵ֖ט בַּ⁠שִׁלּ֑וּם

"and the judge, for the recompense"

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the judge is also asking for the recompense]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 7:3 (#4)
content:
בַּ⁠שִׁלּ֑וּם

"for the recompense"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of recompense, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be paid]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 7:3 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠גָּד֗וֹל דֹּבֵ֨ר הַוַּ֥ת נַפְשׁ֛⁠וֹ ה֖וּא

"and the great one is speaking the desire of his very soul"

Micah is not referring to a specific great one. He means people in positions of power in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and important people are speaking the desire of their very souls]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Micah 7:3 (#6)
content:
הַוַּ֥ת נַפְשׁ֛⁠וֹ ה֖וּא

"the desire of his very soul"

Here, his very soul represents the great one himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of what he himself strongly desires]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 7:3 (#7)
content:
הַוַּ֥ת נַפְשׁ֛⁠וֹ ה֖וּא

"the desire of his very soul"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of desire, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he himself desires]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 7:3 (#8)
content:
וַֽ⁠יְעַבְּתֽוּ⁠הָ

"and they weave it together"

The pronoun they refers to all of the powerful leaders. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and these leaders weave it together]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 7:3 (#9)
content:
וַֽ⁠יְעַבְּתֽוּ⁠הָ

"and they weave it together"

Here Micah is speaking of the plot that these leaders are scheming together as if it were a net that they weave together. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they plot it out together]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 7:4 (#1)
content:
כְּ⁠חֵ֔דֶק

"is} like a brier"

The point of this comparison is that just as a brier wounds anyone who touches it, so is even the best person among these people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [injures anyone who comes near, just as a brier does]

See: Simile

title: Micah 7:4 (#2)
content:
יָשָׁ֖ר מִ⁠מְּסוּכָ֑ה

"the upright, {worse} than a thorn hedge"

The point of this comparison is that just as a thorn hedge injures those who come near it, so is the one who seems to be one of the upright people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the upright person injures people even more than a thorn hedge injures those who come near it]

See: Simile

title: Micah 7:4 (#3)
content:
יָשָׁ֖ר

"the upright"

Micah is using the adjective the upright as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the most honest person]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Micah 7:4 (#4)
content:
י֤וֹם מְצַפֶּ֨י⁠ךָ֙

"The day of your watchers"

Micah is using the term day to refer to a specific time and your watchers represents the prophets, who warned the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The time that your prophets warned you about]

See: Metonymy

title: Micah 7:4 (#5)
content:
מְצַפֶּ֨י⁠ךָ֙ פְּקֻדָּתְ⁠ךָ֣

"your watchers, your visitation"

The pronoun your refers to the people of Israel, whom Micah addresses directly here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your watchers, people of Israel, your visitation]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 7:4 (#6)
content:
פְּקֻדָּתְ⁠ךָ֣

"your visitation"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of visitation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when God comes to punish you]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 7:4 (#7)
content:
עַתָּ֥ה תִהְיֶ֖ה מְבוּכָתָֽ⁠ם

"Now their confusion will be"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of confusion, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When that happens, they will be confused and panic]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 7:5 (#1)
content:
שְׁמֹ֖ר פִּתְחֵי־פִֽי⁠ךָ

"guard the doors of your mouth"

Micah is using guard the doors of your mouth as a common expression of the culture to mean “be very careful about what you say.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you should guard what you say]

See: Idiom

title: Micah 7:6 (#1)
content:
כַּלָּ֖ה בַּ⁠חֲמֹתָ֑⁠הּ

"a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law"

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [a daughter-in-law is rising up against her mother-in-law]

See: Ellipsis

title: Micah 7:6 (#2)
content:
אֹיְבֵ֥י אִ֖ישׁ

"The enemies of a man"

Micah is using the possessive form to describe enemies who are characterized by their relationship to a man. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The ones who oppose a man]

See: Possession

title: Micah 7:6 (#3)
content:
אַנְשֵׁ֥י בֵיתֽ⁠וֹ

"are} the men of his house"

Micah is using the possessive form to describe the men who are characterized by living in his house. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way as modeled in the UST.

See: Possession

title: Micah 7:7 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִי֙ בַּ⁠יהוָ֣ה אֲצַפֶּ֔ה

"But I, I will watch for Yahweh"

Micah is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I will watch already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between himself and the people he has been describing. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But unlike these people, I will watch for Yahweh]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 7:7 (#2)
content:
לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׁעִ֑⁠י

"the God of my salvation"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of salvation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who saves me]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 7:7 (#3)
content:
אֱלֹהָֽ⁠י

"My God"

Moses is not using this possessive form My God to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather Moses is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom I worship,]

See: Possession

title: Micah 7:8 (#1)
content:
אַֽל־תִּשְׂמְחִ֤י אֹיַ֨בְתִּ⁠י֙ לִ֔⁠י כִּ֥י נָפַ֖לְתִּי קָ֑מְתִּי כִּֽי־אֵשֵׁ֣ב בַּ⁠חֹ֔שֶׁךְ יְהוָ֖ה א֥וֹר לִֽ⁠י

"Do not rejoice over me, my enemy! Though I have fallen; I will arise. Though I sit in the darkness; Yahweh {is} a light to me"

In verses 8 through 10 Micah speaks on behalf of his people. If it would be helpful, you could translate the singular pronouns as plurals, as in the UST.

See: Synecdoche

title: Micah 7:8 (#2)
content:
אֹיַ֨בְתִּ⁠י֙

"my enemy"

By my enemy, Micah refers to the nation that Micah foresees will conquer Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you enemy nation of my people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Micah 7:8 (#3)
content:
נָפַ֖לְתִּי קָ֑מְתִּי

"I have fallen; I will arise"

Here Micah is speaking on behalf of the people about suffering defeat as if it were to have fallen down and of recovering as if it were to arise again. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we have suffered disaster; we will be restored]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 7:8 (#4)
content:
אֵשֵׁ֣ב בַּ⁠חֹ֔שֶׁךְ יְהוָ֖ה א֥וֹר לִֽ⁠י

"I sit in the darkness; Yahweh {is} a light to me"

Here Micah is speaking of the trouble his people are experiencing as if it were the darkness and of Yahweh’s help as if it were a light. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are in trouble; Yahweh helps us]

See: Metaphor

title: Micah 7:9 (#1)
content:
זַ֤עַף יְהוָה֙ אֶשָּׂ֔א כִּ֥י חָטָ֖אתִי ל֑⁠וֹ

"I will bear the rage of Yahweh, for I have sinned against him"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because I have sinned against Yahweh, I will bear his rage]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Micah 7:9 (#2)
content:
זַ֤עַף יְהוָה֙

"the rage of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of rage, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how Yahweh rages against me]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Micah 7:9 (#3)
content:
יָרִ֤יב רִיבִ⁠י֙

"he pleads my case"
